title: Statement on due diligence - Introduction
heading: GOV-4 : Statement on due diligence
start_phrase: The financial services sector itself has for years been confronted with many challenges and risks.
summary: Introductory overview of RBI’s due diligence approach in its consolidated non-financial statement, highlighting the sector’s risk context and the need for robust risk management and sustainability. It maps core due diligence elements to specific ESRS disclosures: embedding in governance/strategy (ESRS 2 GOV-2, GOV-3, SBM-3), stakeholder engagement (GOV-2, SBM-2, IRO-1, E1-2, S1-1, S1-2, S4-1, S4-2, G1-1 corporate culture and business conduct, G1-2 supplier relationships), identifying/assessing impacts (SBM-3, IRO-1), taking action (relevant impact/risk/opportunity sections), and tracking/communicating (E1-4, S1-5, GOV-5). It describes preparation and governance: collaborative drafting by Group ESG & Sustainability Management, Group Accounting & Financial Methodologies, and divisions (including Group Risk Controlling, Group People, Culture & Organization, Facility Management); data collection in divisions; use of the Workiva tool for simultaneous editing, tracking, and transparency; approval by division heads, then Management Board and Supervisory Board. It emphasizes statutory compliance and an internal control system (ICS) set by the Management Board for accounting and, prospectively, the non-financial statement to prevent misstatements. Two key risks are identified—omitting material topics and inaccurate data—with mitigations via a pre-report materiality assessment (SBM-3) and dual controls within divisions.
text:
Statement on due diligence
The financial services sector itself has for years been confronted with many challenges and risks. In order to remain profitable 
over the long term, these challenges call for a strong culture of risk management and sustainability. Compliance with 
appropriate due diligence processes is therefore of particular importance. The following overview provides information on 
which sections of the current consolidated non-financial statement contain the core elements of due diligence, i.e. the 
procedures conducted or processes implemented by RBI to identify actual and potential negative impacts on the environment 
and people in connection with its business activities.
Core elements of due diligence Paragraph in consolidated non-financial statement
a) Embedding due diligence in governance, strategy and business model ESRS 2 GOV-2 : Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by 
the undertaking’s administrative, management and supervisory bodies

schemes

and opportunities

S4-2: Processes for engaging with consumers and end-users about impacts
G1-1: Corporate culture  and G1-1: Business conduct policies 
G1-2 : Management of relationships with suppliers
c) Identifying and assessing adverse impacts ESRS 2 SBM-3: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with 
strategy and business model

and opportunities

e) Tracking the effectiveness of these efforts and communicating E1-4:  Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
S1-5:  Targets related to managing material negative impacts, advancing positive 
impacts, and managing material risks and opportunities
GOV-5 : Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting
The consolidated non-financial statement was created in collaboration between Group ESG & Sustainability Management and 
Group Accounting & Financial Methodologies, as well as the individual business divisions. Data collection was carried out in the 
respective business divisions (including Group Risk Controlling, Group ESG & Sustainability Management, Group People, Culture & 
Organization, Facility Management). The consolidated non-financial statement was prepared using the Workiva collaboration 
tool. This tool enables all authorized users to access and edit the document simultaneously, greatly enhancing collaboration, 
automation, and transparency in the consolidated non-financial statement. Additionally, any changes in structure or content 
can be easily implemented and tracked. Once the report is completed, the non-financial statement is approved by the 
responsible division heads and then submitted to the Management Board and the Supervisory Board for review and final 
approval.
A balanced and comprehensive consolidated non-financial statement is a priority for RBI and its governing bodies, requiring 
compliance with all statutory requirements. The Management Board establishes and defines an internal control and risk 
management system for the entire accounting process including in the future the process for the consolidated non-financial 
statement within the company-wide ICS framework. This system is designed to ensure  effective, continuously improving 
controls,  as well as adherence to guidelines and regulations to prevent any unintentional misstatements.Group management report 95
 ·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   
Two risks were identified in the consolidated non-financial statement: the risk of overlooking material topics, leading to an 
incomplete report, and the risk of inaccurate data. To mitigate the first risk, a materiality assessment is conducted before 
report preparation (see chapter SBM-3: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with the strategy and 
business model ), ensuring all relevant topics are identified and addressed. There is a second risk that incorrect data is input 
into the consolidated non-financial statement. To cover this risk, the report’s contents are subjected to dual controls within the 
respective divisions.

title: Risk framework
heading: Risk framework
start_phrase: Risk management is essential for implementing the ESG strategy and the associated risk control measures.
summary:
- Identifies two key risks in the consolidated non-financial statement: missing material topics and inaccurate data.
- Describes mitigations: a pre-report materiality assessment to ensure topic completeness and dual control checks within divisions to ensure data accuracy.
- Presents RBI’s ESG risk framework as integral to the overall risk organization and ESG strategy execution.
- Notes the initial focus on climate and environmental risks (transition and physical) assessed at counterparty level and via materiality assessment and internal/external climate stress tests, with growing emphasis on social and governance risks.
- Details integration of ESG risks into the four pillars of risk management:
  - Identification and definition of ESG risks (climate change, circularity, biodiversity; social and governance risks).
  - Measurement methodologies and analytics (ESG scores, Green Asset Ratio, financed GHG emissions, climate stress testing).
  - Steering approaches reflecting risks and opportunities (sectoral strategies, special policies, prevention of liability, reputational, and greenwashing risks in design).
  - Risk processes and governance (credit process enhancements, ESG Risk Policy Statement).
- Explains that ESG topics are managed through the CRO line organization to embed them in daily business, aligning with ECB and EBA guidance and RBI’s business model.
- States progress tracking via internal ESG KPIs and regular monitoring.
- Confirms the ESG risk framework is reviewed and updated annually based on trends and stakeholder expectations, and approved by the Management Board.
text:
Risk framework
Risk management is essential for implementing the ESG strategy and the associated risk control measures. ESG is part of the 
entire risk organization.
RBI gears its business model to the high-level strategic goal of creating long-term value in line with the principles of 
responsible banking and regulatory requirements. In concrete terms, RBI identifies, acknowledges, and aligns the continuous 
development of its risk management approach with the additional risks originating from ESG. 
Initially, the focus was on tackling climate and environment-related risks (transition and physical risks), not only via an 
assessment at the counterparty level but also by considering the potential impact of those risks stemming from the 
materiality assessment and the internal/external climate stress test. In the meantime, social and governance aspects are also 
gaining increasing importance (as further described in RBI’s risk management approach). 
ESG-related risks have been accounted for by enhancing the existing classical four pillars of risk management on multiple 
operational levels:
· Identification and definition of ESG risks
· Measurement, methodologies and analytics
· Steering approaches, reflecting risks and opportunities 
· Risk processes and governance
ESG-related topics in the CRO area are addressed via the line organization. This ensures complete integration into day-to-day 
business. The aim is to meet the regulatory requirements as set out in the ECB and EBA guidelines on climate and 
environmental risks and at the same time to align the measures with RBI's business model.
When referring to the traditional four pillars of risk management, which are the foundation of the RBI risk m anagement  
approach , RBI focuses on addressing, quantifying, managing and further integrating the respective risks, as well as the 
opportunities. RBI’s progress is measured via the regular monitoring and establishment of internal ESG KPIs. The main topics 
reflected within each pillar are highlighted below:

risksII. Measurement methodologies & 
analyticsIII. Steering approaches, reflecting 
risks & opportunitiesIV. Risk processes and governance
·Climate-related and environmental 
risks·Use of metrics for measurement of 
ESG on a customer and portfolio 
dimension·Sectoral strategies & special policies ·Credit processes enhancement
·Identifying risks according to:
·Climate change
·Circularity
·Biodiversity·Environmental, Social and 
Governance score
·Green Asset Ratio
·Financed GHG emissions·Climate stress testing ·Prevention of liability, reputational 
and greenwashing risk in the design 
phase

The ESG risk framework is intended to ensure  implementation across the four risk management pillars, offering a high-level 
overview and guidance for ongoing and planned risk management activit ies in RBI . These actions are motivated by the 
expectation s of internal and external stakeholders. RBI reviews the framework on a yearly basis, updated to the latest 
available trends and future expectations, and approved by the Management Board. 96 Group  management report

title: Identification of ESG risks
heading: Identification of ESG risks
start_phrase: Proper identification, definition and understanding of ESG risks are crucial.
summary:
- Emphasis on properly identifying, defining, and understanding ESG risks, with initial focus on climate and environmental risks; social and governance risks are gaining prominence amid new regulations (e.g., upcoming EBA guidelines).
- Methodological approach combines qualitative, expert-driven work with quantitative tools: impact and materiality assessments, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests.
- Organization-wide knowledge transfer through mandatory ESG risk training for risk staff and regular training/exchange sessions across RBI and its subsidiaries.
- Environmental risks defined via an outside-in lens: financial impacts from counterparties exposed to climate change and environmental degradation (air/water pollution, water scarcity, land contamination, biodiversity loss, deforestation), leading to physical and transition risks and potentially higher capital needs, costs, revenue losses, and deterioration in credit quality; transmission to traditional risk types (market, liquidity, credit, operational) noted.
- Social risks framed as financial impacts from misuse of human capital (working conditions, health and safety, diversity, training, inclusiveness, equality, community programs); ESG scoring incorporates country-specific social standards, affecting customer scores.
- Governance risks tied to counterparties’ governance practices and integration of ESG in policies (executive pay, board structure/diversity, shareholder rights, anti-bribery/corruption, compliance, ethical standards including data ethics, fair tax strategy).
- Measurement methodologies and analytics focus on creating, collecting, and sourcing ESG data, with references to estimation and outcome uncertainty.
- Steering and strategy: commitments and policies addressing thermal coal, nuclear power, arms and war material, and gambling; development of sector-specific policies for high CO2 emitters and sectors with negative impacts on circularity and biodiversity; references to related policy and climate stress testing disclosures.
text:
Identification of ESG risks
Proper identification, definition and understanding of ESG risks are crucial. In the first phase, RBI placed particular focus on 
climate-related and environmental risks, although social and governmental risks are also gaining increasing attention in 
internal risk initiatives, especially with new regulations such as the upcoming new EBA guidelines. An initial qualitative and 
expert-driven approach has been further supported by quantitative assessments including impact analysis, materiality 
assessments, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests. 
The definition of ESG risks and the transmission channels to traditional risk types are explained in more detail in the following 
chapter. The knowledge gained is transferred across the organization (including all of RBI’s subsidiaries) through different 
training activities (training sessions for new topics, regular exchange sessions, etc.). ESG risk training has become mandatory in 
the risk area.
Calculating financed  emission s helps RBI in identifying the most carbon-intensive industries in its non-retail portfolio. A more 
detailed description and results are included under the chapter  E1-6: Gross GHG emissions of categories Scope 1, 2, and 3 as 
well as total GHG emissions . 
Environmental risk 
Climate and environmental risks are driven by environmental factors (E risks). In the outside-in view, these risks should be 
understood as the financial risks posed by RBI’s exposures to counterparties that may potentially contribute to or be affected 
by climate change or adaption, and other forms of environmental degradation (such as air pollution, water pollution, scarcity 
of fresh water, land contamination, biodiversity loss and deforestation). Related to this, RBI and its customers have to comply 
with additional political and social demands, otherwise RBI’s portfolio may face additional risks relating to physical damage or 
transition. 
As such, E risks can result in additional capital requirements, expenditures and potential losses of revenue, which may lead to a 
deterioration in the respective credit standing and therefore have an adverse effect on the business, financial position and 
results of RBI’s operations. Further information on the different climate-related risks and their transmission channels to the 
traditional risk types (market, liquidity, credit and operational risks) can be found in the section on the assessment of the 
materiality of climate and environment-related risks. 
Social and governance risks 
These risks are addressed in RBI’s internal risk framework, building on the existing structure and internal information. RBI 
continuously updates and refines its approach to measure these risks and aligns itself with the latest industry standards.
· Social risks arise from the financial impact generated by the misuse of human capital, e.g. regarding the rights, well-
being and interests of people and communities. This could refer to working conditions, health and safety, employee 
relations and diversity, employee training, inclusiveness, equality, or community programs. Regarding all E, S and G-
related topics, RBI also includes the local conditions in the respective country. For example, countries with low (or 
high) standards in social aspects such as human rights have a lower (or higher) score. This also impacts the ESG 
score of the customer: identical corporates with different country risk may have different ESG scores due to varying 
country scores. 
· Governance risks refer to the governance practices of RBI’s counterparties, including the inclusion of ESG factors in 
policies and procedures under the governance of the counterparties. This may include, but is not limited to, executive 
pay, board diversity and structure, shareholder rights, bribery and corruption, compliance, ethical standards (e.g. 
data ethics), fair tax strategy, etc.

title: Measurement methodologies & analytics
heading: Measurement methodologies & analytics
start_phrase: This chapter focuses on data creation, collection and data sourcing.
summary:
- The document outlines RBI’s approach to identifying, defining, and understanding ESG risks, with an initial emphasis on climate-related and environmental risks, while increasingly integrating social and governance aspects in line with evolving regulations (e.g., upcoming EBA guidelines).
- RBI complements qualitative, expert-driven assessments with quantitative tools such as impact and materiality analyses, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests; ESG risk training is mandatory across the risk function and shared group-wide.
- Financed emissions are used to pinpoint carbon-intensive industries in the non-retail portfolio, with detailed results referenced in a dedicated emissions chapter.
- Environmental risks are framed from an outside-in perspective as financial risks arising from counterparties’ exposure to climate change and environmental degradation (e.g., pollution, water scarcity, biodiversity loss), as well as compliance pressures; these can translate into physical and transition risks affecting capital, costs, revenues, and credit quality, with transmission to market, liquidity, credit, and operational risks.
- Social risks relate to the financial impacts of mismanaging human capital (e.g., labor conditions, health and safety, diversity, inclusion), with country-specific social standards influencing customer ESG scores.
- Governance risks cover counterparties’ governance practices (e.g., executive pay, board structure, shareholder rights, anti-corruption, compliance, data ethics, fair tax), including how ESG is embedded in policies and procedures.
- Measurement and analytics emphasize data creation, collection, and sourcing, with further detail provided in a chapter on estimation sources and uncertainty.
- Steering actions include commitments and policies for sensitive sectors (thermal coal, nuclear power, arms and war material, gambling) and evolving sector-specific policies targeting high CO2 emitters and activities with adverse circularity/biodiversity impacts; references are provided to chapters on climate policies and stress test results.
text:
This chapter focuses on data creation, collection and data sourcing. For details see chapter Sources of estimation and 
outcome uncertainty .

title: Steering approaches, reflecting risk and opportunities
heading: Steering approaches, reflecting risk and opportunities
start_phrase:
Due to its market position RBI takes responsibility to redefine and reshape its business in line with the latest market and 
regulatory requirements.
summary:
- Focus and scope: RBI’s ESG risk framework prioritizes climate-related and environmental risks while increasingly integrating social and governance risks in line with evolving regulations (e.g., upcoming EBA guidelines).
- Risk identification and assessment: Starts with a qualitative, expert-driven approach, now complemented by quantitative tools such as impact and materiality assessments, financed emissions calculations, and climate stress tests; transmission channels to traditional risk types are defined and elaborated separately.
- Organizational enablement: ESG risk knowledge is cascaded across RBI and its subsidiaries via training and exchange sessions; ESG risk training is mandatory for risk staff.
- Financed emissions: Used to identify carbon-intensive sectors in the non-retail portfolio; detailed metrics are referenced in chapter E1-6 (Scope 1–3 and total GHG emissions).
- Environmental (E) risks: Defined via an outside-in lens as financial risks from counterparties exposed to climate change and environmental degradation (e.g., pollution, water scarcity, biodiversity loss, deforestation), including physical and transition risk drivers that can affect capital needs, costs, revenues, and credit standing; links to market, liquidity, credit, and operational risk are detailed elsewhere.
- Social (S) risks: Cover financial impacts of misuse of human capital (e.g., labor conditions, health and safety, diversity, training, inclusion); ESG scoring incorporates country-level social standards, so identical corporates may differ in scores by jurisdiction.
- Governance (G) risks: Concern counterparties’ governance quality and integration of ESG into policies (e.g., executive pay, board diversity, shareholder rights, anti-bribery, compliance, ethics, data ethics, tax fairness).
- Measurement methodologies and analytics: Emphasis on data creation, collection, and sourcing; further detail in “Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty.”
- Steering and sector policies: RBI commits to aligning business with regulatory/market expectations, with specific commitments in thermal coal, nuclear power, arms/war material, and gambling; evolving sector-specific policies target high-CO2 and high negative impacts on circularity and biodiversity.
- Disclosures and references: Policies on climate mitigation/adaptation in chapter E1-2; climate stress testing results in the Climate stress testing chapter.
text:
Due to its market position RBI takes responsibility to redefine and reshape its business in line with the latest market and 
regulatory requirements. Commitments have been made in the areas of thermal coal, nuclear power, arms and war material, 
and gambling. Efforts have also been taken to (re)define the approach to industries with high CO2 emissions and/or high 
negative impacts on circularity and biodiversity by further developing sector-specific group policies.
An overview of the existing policies related to climate change mitigation and adaption can be found in chapter E1-2: Policies 
related to climate change mitigation and adaptation . The results of the climate stress test is disclosed in the chapter Climate 
stress testing . Group management report 97

title: Risk processes and governance
heading: Risk processes and governance
start_phrase: The Management Board is the most senior decision-making body for ESG-related strategies, policies and commitments.
summary:
- Governance structure: ESG strategies, policies and commitments are led by the Management Board, with environmental risk tools and reports pre-approved by the Group Risk Committee and supported by a cross-functional Sustainability Committee.
- ESG risk integration: ESG risks are treated as cross-dimensional drivers embedded across market, operational, liquidity and credit risk, with measurement over short-, medium- and long-term horizons. Materiality assessments inform implementation and ongoing enhancement of the ICAAP.
- Risk appetite and ICAAP: Group risk tolerance is set below 100% of overall risk capacity. Transition and physical (flood) climate risks, informed by climate stress tests, are recognized as deductions from Pillar 2 internal capital (from Q1 2022). Environmental risk drivers have been included in group risk assessment since 2021, and are budgeted within the short-term (up to three years) risk appetite.
- Methodologies and standards: Scenario analysis and materiality assessments use NGFS frameworks and scenarios aligned with EU climate objectives; physical risk impacts are assessed under NGFS transition scenarios. Financed emissions reduction targets align with EU 2030 goals. Additional standards are set out in the RBI Group ESG Rulebook.
- Tools and policies (as of end-2024): ESG score; Green Asset Ratio (GAR); financed GHG emissions; sector business policies (nuclear energy, steel, oil & gas, real estate and construction, thermal coal); RBI Group ESG Rulebook; ESG risk framework; climate stress test methodology and results; ICAAP treatment of transition and physical risks.
- Reporting: ESG risk reporting is embedded in the risk controlling framework and presented regularly to the Group Risk Committee. Quarterly reports include financed emissions, physical risk/vulnerability, energy efficiency distribution, exposure to top polluters, ESG rating distribution, and GAR; climate stress tests are reported annually.
- Sustainability strategy (SBM-1): RBI defines sustainability as responsible corporate activity for long-term economic success while considering social and environmental aspects, embedding it in leadership and management. Through an ESG & Sustainability Policy, RBI focuses on areas with significant impacts on economy, environment and people (including human rights), aiming to enhance positive impacts, reduce negatives, and measure both.
- Strategic drivers and focus: Sustainability is integrated into business strategy, driven by regulation, supervisory expectations, and stakeholder demands (investors, customers, employees). The group-wide strategy “RBI creates sustainable value” centers on three action areas—responsible banker, fair partner, engaged citizen—covering economy, environment and society, and is operationalized via nine core action areas that are continuously refined with stakeholder input.
text:
Risk processes and governance
The Management Board is the most senior decision-making body for ESG-related strategies, policies and commitments. 
However, reports and the main tools used to manage and supervise environmental-related risks are pre-approved by the 
Group Risk Committee. In addition to the regular Risk Committee structure, the Management Board is supported in its ESG 
decisions by the cross-functional Sustainability Committee. 
From a risk management and supervision perspective, environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks are viewed as cross-
dimensional risks that affect all areas of risk management. As such, the ESG risks have been included in the group risk 
framework and methods as drivers of existing risk types. The materiality assessment described in a separate chapter forms 
the basis for implementation of the ICAAP and is to be adapted accordingly in the coming years as methodologies and 
common practices are further developed. Each relevant risk department (market, operational, liquidity and credit risk) is 
responsible for measuring environmentally-driven risks over each specific time horizon (long term, short term and medium 
term). The risk framework and processes are continuously updated, refined and adjusted to the current standards. 
As part of the RBI risk strategy, the overarching group risk tolerance is set at a threshold of <100 per cent of overall risk 
capacity. The impact of transition risks and physical (flood) risks on the risk profile has been introduced to the economic 
perspective of the ICAAP as an item for deduction from the pillar 2 capital. This item has been defined on the basis of the 
climate risk stress test result. As such, these risks are included in the overarching risk appetite budgeting or are bundled 
together with all other risk types measured under pillar 2 for the short-term horizon (up to three years). Finally, the results of 
the yearly materiality assessment are included for further development in the ICAAP framework.
In the identification and management of environmental factors and risk, RBI aims to make use of market best practice and 
develop methods in line with applicable international benchmarks. Most importantly, for the environmental risk RBI bases its 
scenario analysis, which also feeds into the materiality assessment of climate and environmental risks, on the NGFS-
framework (network for greening the financial system), and the scenarios developed by NGFS  to work out various transitions 
that are in line with the EU’s climate change objectives  (see chapter Climate stress test). Also when assessing physical risks, the 
impact is evaluated under different transition scenarios in line with the NGFS framework . In addition to this, RBI’s reduction 
targets on financed emissions have been set to be in line with the EU 2030 targets  (see chapter E1-1: Transition plan for climate 
change mitigation ). For additional international standards applied within RBI’s ESG risk framework see chapter RBI Group ESG 
rulebook . 
The main tools for managing and supervising environment-related risks approved by the RBI Management Board as of year-
end 2024 are:
· Environmental, social and governance score
· Green Asset Ratio (GAR)
· Financed GHG emissions
· Business policy on nuclear energy
· Business policy on steel 
· Business policy on oil & gas 
· Business policy on real estate and construction
· Business policy on thermal coal 
· RBI Group ESG Rulebook 
· ESG risk framework
· Climate stress test methodology and results
· ICAAP: from Q1 2022 onwards, transition and physical risks have been defined as items for deduction from the pillar 2 
internal capital. Since 2021, environmental risk drivers have been included in the group risk assessment.
Regarding specific reporting, ESG risk reports are continuously included in the risk controlling reporting framework. Reports 
currently implemented and reported regularly to the Group Risk Committee include: the financed emission calculation, physical 
risk assessment/vulnerability, energy efficiency distribution, climate stress tests, exposure towards top polluters, ESG rating 
distribution, and the GAR results report. With the exception of climate risk stress tests, which are reported annually, ESG 
reports are presented to the Group Risk Committee on a quarterly basis. 98 Group  management report

title: RBI’s understanding of sustainability
heading: RBI’s u nderstanding of sustainability
start_phrase: Sustainability is a fundamental principle for RBI and a measure of corporate success.
summary:
- RBI positions sustainability as a core corporate principle and a measure of success, combining financial performance with social responsibility built over 130+ years.
- Defines sustainability as responsible corporate activity that delivers long-term economic results while considering key social and environmental aspects, linked to corporate culture.
- Embeds sustainability into leadership, management structures, processes, and daily business activities; it is an explicit part of the overall business strategy and value chain.
- Establishes an ESG & Sustainability Policy to guide strategic integration of sustainability across operations.
- Focuses on three strategic responsibility areas—responsible banker, fair partner, engaged citizen—each aligned to the pillars of economy, environment, and society.
- Aims to prioritize areas with significant impacts on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights), enhance positive impacts, reduce negative ones, and develop metrics to measure and verify outcomes.
- Seeks to create long-term corporate value while contributing to sustainable societal development.
- Identifies key drivers for a concrete sustainability strategy: evolving regulations, supervisory expectations, and growing demands from investors, customers (for sustainable products/services), and employees (for real impact and results).
- Introduces a group-wide strategy, “RBI creates sustainable value,” comprising the three action areas and nine core action areas for sustainability management, with priorities updated continuously based on stakeholder perspectives.
text:
Sustainability is a fundamental principle for RBI and a measure 
of corporate success. For over 130 years, Raiffeisen has 
combined financial success with socially responsible action.
· RBI understands sustainability to mean responsible 
corporate activities for a long-term, economically 
positive result in consideration of key societal and 
environmental aspects. See also chapter G1-1: 
Corporate culture
· RBI combines financial success with social 
responsibility by anchoring sustainability as a fixed 
component of its business and by practicing 
sustainability as an integral leadership and 
management responsibility, in addition to taking 
key sustainability aspects into consideration in its 
business activities.
· RBI is therefore committed to aligning the 
management structures and processes with this 
attitude. In the three strategic sustainability areas of responsibility – responsible banker, fair partner, and engaged 
citizen – which are closely linked to the business activities, RBI endeavors to professionally and effectively apply the 
values and competences to fostering sustainable development both in RBI and in society.  
In an ESG & Sustainability Policy, RBI has formulated the strategic approach to pursuing sustainability and its intent to 
integrate it into business activities.
The goal is to concentrate on those areas which have a significant impact on the economy, the environment and people, 
including human rights. This requires RBI to continuously improve the positive impacts of the business activities while reducing 
the more negative aspects, and develop ways to measure and verify both. This approach aims to increase RBI’s long-term 
value while also actively contributing to the sustainable development of society. 
Sustainability is part of RBI’s business strategy. A sustainability strategy with concrete goals is a necessity primarily arising 
from new regulations, expectations of supervisory authorities, and the demands of investors, customers and society. 
Consumers are demanding more and more sustainable products and services. Employees are demanding more from 
companies and choosing their jobs based not only on a company’s core values, but also on its actual impact and results.

title: Core action areas of RBI’s sustainability strategy
heading: Core action areas of RBI’s sustainability str ategy
start_phrase: The most effective leverage for a bank is in its core business, namely in granting loans and investing funds.
summary:
- Outlines RBI’s sustainability matrix across Economy, Society, and Environment, structured around three roles:
  - Responsible banker: value creation, social and ecological product responsibility (consumer protection, data protection, transparent information; compliance with environmental laws and conventions; integrating environmental impacts in finance and products).
  - Fair partner: fair business and operating practices, stakeholder inclusion, and in-house ecology (anti-corruption, transparent reporting, attractive employer; systematic stakeholder engagement; reducing own environmental footprint and meeting group climate targets).
  - Engaged citizen: sustainable entrepreneurship, active civil society, environmentally friendly society (supporting sustainable finance frameworks and social initiatives; financial literacy and volunteering; climate action, biodiversity, and ecosystem protection).
- Emphasizes core-business leverage in lending and investing to build long-term resilience, avoid social and environmental risks, and advance higher standards; grounded in trust and reliability.
- Confirms RBI’s commitment to sustainable development in Austria and CEE, making ESG central to strategy with measurable positive impacts, science-based CO2 targets, alignment with EU ESG regulations, and adherence to UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Describes governance and execution: assessing positive/negative ESG impacts, setting improvement goals, adapting products/services, fostering a sustainability-oriented culture, proactive stakeholder engagement, and transparent reporting.
- Details the climate and environmental business strategy:
  - 2024 update with Management Board–approved emissions targets.
  - Gradual integration of qualitative/quantitative criteria into business processes to manage the portfolio sustainably.
  - Reducing exposure to companies that fail climate/environmental criteria or lack credible transition pathways.
  - Supporting customers’ climate and ecological transition through transition pathways, ESG expertise, and sustainable finance solutions to increase climate-friendly transactions.
  - Regular reviews reflecting scientific advances, portfolio ESG insights, and clients’ transformation progress; sector-specific tailoring where needed.
- Introduces three strategic pillars aligned with regulatory requirements and UNEP FI commitments; the first pillar focuses on Paris Agreement alignment by:
  - Embedding climate and environmental factors in lending decisions, risk and operational control, and resource allocation.
  - Expanding the use of assets for sustainable financing products.
text:
The most effective leverage for a bank is in its core business, namely in granting loans and investing funds. RBI takes the 
greatest possible care to structure its business and business relationships for long-term resilience, to avoid social and 
environmental risks and to take advantage of opportunities to improve environmental protection and social standards. Trust 
and reliability have always formed part of RBI’s fundamental principles.
As one of the leading banks in Central and Eastern Europe as well as in Austria, RBI has confirmed its commitment to 
sustainable development. RBI aims to make ESG-related activities and business a key part of its business strategy in Austria 
and its home markets. It aims to achieve measurable positive impacts within the framework of a sustainable transformation. 
Accordingly, it sets science-based CO 2 targets and follows the European ESG regulations and its own sustainable pathway . The 
management of its business activities is guided by  the UNEP FI’s  Principles for Responsible Banking. In line with this, RBI pursues 
a sustainable business strategy. It evaluates the positive and negative ESG impacts of its business activities, sets goals for 
improvement, adapts its product and service offerings, ensures holistic governance and culture, conducts a proactive 
stakeholder engagement process, and reports transparently. RBI endeavors to support its customers in their transition to a 
sustainable future, in particular with regard to climate and the environment.

title: RBI’s climate and environmental business strategy
heading: RBI’s climate and environmental business strategy
start_phrase: In 2024, the climate and environmental business strategy was further developed by setting emissions targets which were approved by the Management Board.
summary:
- Outlines RBI’s sustainability matrix across economy, society and environment, detailing responsibilities in core banking (value creation), social and ecological product responsibility, fair business practices, stakeholder engagement, in‑house ecology, sustainable entrepreneurship, active civil society and an environmentally friendly society.
- Emphasizes the bank’s greatest leverage through core activities—lending and investing—aimed at long‑term resilience, avoidance of social and environmental risks, and seizing sustainability opportunities, underpinned by trust and reliability.
- Confirms commitment to integrate ESG into strategy and operations in Austria and CEE, pursue measurable positive impacts, set science‑based CO2 targets, follow EU ESG regulations, and align with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Describes a climate and environmental business strategy with 2024 Board‑approved emissions targets, integrating qualitative and quantitative criteria into processes to manage portfolios sustainably and limit exposure to companies lacking credible transition pathways.
- Details continuous review of the strategy based on scientific advances, portfolio ESG insights, and client transformation progress, with sector‑specific adaptation.
- Presents three strategic pillars:
  1) Align portfolios with the Paris Agreement by embedding climate and environmental factors in lending, risk, operations and resource allocation, and growing sustainable financing assets.
  2) Support clients’ transition via expertise and practical, innovative sustainable products and services, prioritizing positive environmental and social impacts in CEE.
  3) Advance sustainable finance through robust ESG expertise and governance, including ESG policies, an ESG risk framework and greenwashing prevention processes.
- Highlights corporate and institutional client offering: tailored sustainable finance instruments (loans, bonds, promissory notes, guarantees, derivatives), including sustainability‑linked, ESG rating‑linked and use‑of‑proceeds formats, aligned with EU rules and LMA/ICMA standards.
- Stresses collaborative KPI setting for ESG‑linked financings to ensure materiality and ambition; support spans all sectors, from critical (e.g., oil and gas) to renewables.
- Describes roles across transactions (arranger, bookrunner, sustainability structuring advisor, lender) and comprehensive client support on EU Taxonomy alignment, access to subsidies, ESG ratings, second‑party opinions, SBTi/net‑zero topics and portfolio decarbonization strategies.
- Notes stakeholder engagement, transparency, data protection, anti‑corruption, and internal environmental measures to meet group climate targets, alongside initiatives to promote financial literacy and broader societal and environmental stewardship.
text:
In 2024, the climate and environmental business strategy was further developed by setting emissions targets which were 
approved by the Management Board. For more details please refer to chapter E1-4: Targets related to climate change 
mitigation and adaptation .
RBI set itself the target of gradually implementing qualitative and quantitative criteria in order to integrate its climate and 
environmental business strategy into its business processes. This is intended to enable it to manage the portfolio sustainably 
and to reduce interactions with companies that do not meet climate and environmental criteria and/or economic 
expectations, or that do not pursue any transition pathway.
As a responsible banker, RBI focuses on supporting its customers in their climate and ecological transition. Customers are 
encouraged to work on a targeted basis towards improving their climate and environmental performance by developing and 
following a transition pathway. RBI also offers customers extensive ESG expertise, and practical and innovative sustainable 
financial products and services, thereby contributing to increasing the proportion of climate-friendly transactions.
The climate and environmental business strategy is subject to regular reviews,  where RBI considers not only the scientific 
advances and the updated ESG findings from its portfolios, but also the transformation progress made by its customers. Given 
that its customers and stakeholders are from a very diverse range of sectors, not all elements of the strategy can be fully 
applied to each sector, and some elements may have to be adapted to the respective level of the sectors and markets.
RBI’s climate and environmental strategy is based on three pillars, which are consistent with both its voluntary commitments 
under the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and also with the regulatory requirements.
The first pillar is focused on aligning the bank’s portfolio with the goals of the Paris Agreement. RBI analyzes the impacts of, 
the weak points of and the opportunities presented by its business activities from a climate and environmental perspective. In 
doing so, it considers climate and environmental factors in lending decisi ons, risk and operational control, and when allocating 
resources. It will also increase the use of assets for sustainable financing products. In 2024, the climate and environmental 
business strategy was further developed by setting emissions targets which were approved by the Management Board. For 
more details please refer to chapter E1-4: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation .100 Group  management report
·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   The second pillar focuses on supporting RBI’s customers on their journey towards climate and environmental transition. RBI 
therefore offers its professional expertise to its corporate and institutional clients as well as its retail customers, along with 
practical and innovative financial products and services. It is increasing investments in areas with positive impacts on the 
environment and on society, with a special focus on the region in which it operates, namely Central and Eastern Europe.
In the third pillar, RBI is driving forward the transition to sustainable financing, based on current ESG expertise and ESG 
governance. In order to make a credible contribution to the climate and ecological turnaround, it is crucially important for it to 
develop, maintain and pass on expert knowledge. The establishment of a series of ESG policies and appropriate governance 
(e.g. the ESG risk framework or the process to prevent greenwashing) are a key element of RBI’s strategy and support it in its 
endeavors.

title: Corporate & institutional clients business
heading: Corporate & institutional clients business
start_phrase: RBI serves around 134,000 corporate clients across CEE (including medium-sized businesses, large local companies, international corporations and local authorities) as well as local and international institutional clients.
summary:
- RBI’s second pillar centers on helping customers transition to climate- and environment-friendly practices by providing expertise, innovative financial products, and increased impact investments, with a focus on Central and Eastern Europe.
- The third pillar advances sustainable financing through strong ESG expertise and governance, including establishing ESG policies such as an ESG risk framework and anti-greenwashing processes, and building/maintaining internal knowledge.
- Corporate and institutional clients: RBI serves ~134,000 clients across CEE (from mid-sized firms to international corporations and public sector), offering tailored solutions in financing, capital markets advisory, risk hedging, and transaction banking.
- Sustainable finance offering: wide range of instruments (bonds, promissory notes, syndicated/bilateral loans) linked to ESG ratings, sustainability targets, or use-of-proceeds; support in identifying/defining sustainable transactions aligned with EU regulations and LMA/ICMA standards; EU Taxonomy alignment and internal green/social/sustainable definitions.
- KPI setting: collaborative definition of material, ambitious ESG KPIs tied to clients’ sustainability and business strategies, with annual targets aimed at demonstrable improvement.
- Sector coverage: tailored solutions across all sectors, including critical (e.g., oil and gas) and non-critical (e.g., renewables), ensuring clarity on market standards, requirements, and best practices.
- Transaction roles and formats: acts as arranger, bookrunner, sustainability structuring advisor, and lender; provides loans, promissory notes, bonds, guarantees, derivatives; supports sustainability-linked, ESG rating-linked, and use-of-proceeds formats.
- Additional client support: guidance on EU Taxonomy, access to subsidized financing and EU/Austria programs; assistance with ESG ratings and second-party opinions; advisory on net zero and Science Based Targets initiative.
- Capacity building and strategy: delivers ESG education for institutional clients; supports strategic credit portfolio transformation toward carbon neutrality and SDGs; helps develop ESG and sustainable financing strategies, shift internal perspectives, and manage ongoing ESG processes and trends.
text:
RBI serves around 134,000 corporate clients across CEE (including medium-sized businesses, large local companies, 
international corporations and local authorities) as well as local and international institutional clients. Its product range 
encompasses a broad spectrum of tailored solutions in the areas of finance, capital market advisory and risk hedging as well 
as an extensive selection of transaction banking solutions (clearing, settlement and payment services, trade and export 
finance).
RBI offers support for various sustainable financing options aligned with the business model and sustainability strategy of its 
customers. These sustainable financing options cover a wide range of financial instruments (bonds, promissory notes, 
syndicated loans, bilateral facilities, etc.) characterized by their linkage to ESG ratings or sustainability targets, or by 
demonstration of the use of proceeds.
RBI’s Sustainable Finance experts support corporate and institutional customers in their transformation by identifying and 
defining sustainable transactions.The basis for this assessment of financial products and services includes both the regulatory 
framework of the EU and the international market standards such as those of the Loan Market Association and the 
International Capital Markets Association. RBI supports its customers in verifying the suitability of various projects and 
activities with regard to EU Taxonomy compliance and RBI’s internal definitions of green, social or sustainable transactions. 
When engaging in dialog with customers on ESG-linked products, it is especially important to jointly define material KPIs that 
are important for the customer’s sustainability and business strategy. When establishing the annual target values, care is 
taken to ensure a certain degree of ambition and that the ESG KPIs represent a significant improvement in the customer’s 
sustainability position.
Sustainable financial products can be tailored to the individual customers so that they have a positive impact in terms of ESG 
criteria. RBI supports customers in all sectors – in critical sectors such as oil and gas, and through to non-critical sectors such 
as renewable energy – and in doing so, addresses each individual customer’s respective challenges and opportunities. With all 
sustainable financing transactions, RBI’s Sustainable Finance experts always endeavor to provide corporate and institutional 
customers with a clear understanding of market standards and requirements, as well as best practices.
RBI supports customers during financing transactions:
· In all roles – as arranger, book runner, sustainability structuring advisor and lender
· Through various financing instruments such as loans, promissory notes, bonds, guarantees and derivatives 
· In various forms of sustainable financing, including sustainability-linked and ESG rating-linked formats as well as 
formats where the financing is primarily dedicated to sustainable investments.
In addition to sustainable finance, RBI supports its customers on the EU Taxonomy (where applicable), subsidized financing and 
corresponding subsidy programs in Austria and in the EU.
RBI also assists customers on different ESG ratings and supports them in the verification process for obtaining a second party 
opinion. More in-depth subject-specific advice can be provided where necessary, for example, with regard to net zero matters 
or the Science Based Targets initiative.
Furthermore, RBI supports institutional customers with tailor-made, educational sessions to raise awareness on ESG topics, 
provide updates on ongoing sustainability trends and to change the mindset towards being a sustainable banker. The ESG 
experts also assist with the strategic transformation of the customers’ credit portfolios to achieve carbon neutrality and 
compliance with sustainable development goals. RBI specifically provides support in assessing and developing ESG strategies, 
developing a sustainable financing strategy, changing the internal perspective, as well as support for ongoing ESG-related 
processes and sustainability trends.Group management report 101
 ·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024

title: Retail business
heading: Retail business
start_phrase: RBI provides services to around 18 million retail, private banking and small business customers, offering a broad product range (e.g. account packages, clearing, settlement and payment services, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgage loans and investment products).
summary:
- RBI’s retail segment serves ~18 million retail, private banking, and small business customers with a broad product suite: account packages, payments, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgages, and investment products.
- In Austria, retail investment advisory and asset management are provided via Kathrein Privatbank; housing loans via Raiffeisen Bausparkasse; card business at RBI’s head office.
- Responsible banking is embedded in the Group Strategic Roadmap (since 2023), focusing on supporting customers’ green transition through:
  - Tools to understand customer carbon footprints.
  - Expanded sustainability-oriented products with environmental and social impact.
  - Growth targets for green and social lending (green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgages) to private individuals and small businesses.
- Investment products:
  - Advisory for funds, certificates, and green bond issuance.
  - Sustainable investment of customer deposits primarily via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft (Raiffeisen Capital Management), offering securities and real estate funds and investment management.
  - Sales focus on Austria with key markets in Italy, Germany, and CEE; Austrian distribution via Raiffeisen Banking Group, and local partnerships abroad.
  - Ongoing development of sustainable strategies emphasizing proprietary research and stakeholder engagement; sustainable products used as a key client interface and know-how transfer tool.
  - Kathrein Privatbank provides wealth management, family consulting, sustainable investment, and financing.
- International leasing business across CEE and Austria covering:
  - Vehicles (cars, trucks, trailers)
  - Equipment (e.g., forklifts, batteries)
  - Photovoltaic plants for corporate self-use (with partners)
  - Real estate mainly in Austria via PPPs
  - Rising ESG transactions across categories, with priority on e-vehicle leasing and potential growth in e-trucks/trailers; long-term goal to increase ESG-eligible new business annually.
- Societal aspects in core business:
  - Commitment to responsible sales and marketing aligned with regulation and stakeholder expectations.
  - Strong data protection and cybersecurity practices.
  - Non-discrimination and respectful customer treatment per the RBI Code of Conduct, supported by initiatives and multi-channel access.
  - Link to broader social inclusion efforts for consumers and end-users.
text:
Retail business
RBI provides services to around 18 million retail, private banking and small business customers, offering a broad product range 
(e.g. account packages, clearing, settlement and payment services, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgage loans and 
investment products). In Austria, RBI performs investment advisory and asset management services for retail customers via its 
subsidiary Kathrein Privatbank Aktiengesellschaft, provides housing loans via its building society Raiffeisen Bausparkasse 
Gesellschaft m.b.H. and card business at its head office.
Since 2023, responsible banking also evolved further in the retail strategy and is one of the key elements of the Group Strategic 
Roadmap of retail banking. RBI is focussed on supporting its customers in their green transition. It developed solutions which 
aim at better understanding customers’ carbon footprints and provided products with an environmental and social positive 
impact that, for the first time, allow retail customers to receive a superior supply of sustainability-oriented solutions. RBI aims 
to further increase new green and social loan sales to private individuals and small-business customers, and therefore advise 
its customers on the possibility of green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgage loans.

text:
Business on investment products
On the investment side,  RBI offers advisory services for the fund and certificates business as well as for the issuance of green 
bonds. Sustainable investing of customer deposits at RBI AG is in large part effected via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft 
m.b.H. , which offers securities and real estate investment funds as well as investment management products to institutional 
and private customers under the brand name Raiffeisen Capital Management (RCM). Sales are focused on Austria, and the key 
markets also include Italy, Germany and CEE. In Austria, sales are effected via Raiffeisen Banking Group Austria. In other 
countries, sales cooperations exist with local partners. The sustainable investment strategies and processes are continuously 
being developed, with a focus on proprietary research and the topic of stakeholder engagement. Sustainable product solutions 
play a key role in contact with customers, as this also results in a transfer of know-how.
Kathrein Privatbank Aktiengesellschaft offers services relating to wealth management, family consulting services, sustainable 
investment and financing.

title: International leasing business
heading: International leasing business
start_phrase: There has been growth in the level of ESG transactions in all business categories and the outlook prioritizes car leasing, especially e-vehicles, in cooperation with vehicle manufacturers.
summary:
- Scope of RBI’s retail operations: serves ~18 million retail, private banking, and small-business customers with accounts, payments, consumer finance, car leasing, mortgages, and investment products; in Austria, investment advisory/asset management via Kathrein Privatbank, housing loans via Raiffeisen Bausparkasse, and card business at head office.
- Integration of responsible banking since 2023: retail strategy prioritizes supporting customers’ green transition, including tools to understand carbon footprints and a broad suite of sustainability-oriented products; focus on growing green and social lending (e.g., green unsecured purpose loans and green mortgages) with targeted advice.
- Investment products and sustainable investing: advisory for funds, certificates, and green bond issuance; sustainable investment of deposits mainly via Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft (Raiffeisen Capital Management) offering securities and real estate funds and investment management for institutional and private clients; primary markets Austria, Italy, Germany, and CEE; distribution via Raiffeisen Banking Group Austria and local partners; ongoing enhancement of sustainable strategies with proprietary research and stakeholder engagement; sustainable products used as a vehicle for client education and knowledge transfer.
- Private banking services: Kathrein Privatbank provides wealth management, family consulting, sustainable investment, and financing solutions.
- International leasing business: active across CEE and Austria in four categories—vehicles (cars, trucks, trailers), equipment (e.g., forklifts, batteries), photovoltaic plants for corporate own use, and real estate (mainly via PPP in Austria); increasing ESG transaction share, with strategic emphasis on e-vehicles in partnership with manufacturers and emerging potential in e-trucks/trailers; long-term goal to grow ESG-eligible new business annually.
- Societal considerations in core business: commitment to responsible sales and marketing, strict data protection and security compliance, and non-discrimination per the RBI Code of Conduct; inclusive service delivery across channels and initiatives aligned with social inclusion.
text:
International leasing business 
· RBI’s leasing business spans the CEE region and Austria, covering four main categories
· cars, trucks and other vehicles (trailers)
· forklifts and other equipment (e.g. batteries)
· photovoltaic plants for corporate own use (cooperation with relevant partners)
· real estate mainly in Austria via PPP (private public partnerships) 
There has been growth in the level of ESG transactions in all business categories and the outlook prioritizes car leasing, 
especially e-vehicles, in cooperation with vehicle manufacturers. E-trucks and trailers might become an important driver of the 
business. The long-term goal for the leasing business remains to increase ESG-eligible new business volumes year-on-year.

text:
Societal aspects in the core business
Considering societal aspects in the core business and thus knowing and incorporating the societal needs of customers and end 
consumers is important to RBI. Responsible sales practices and marketing are not only strictly regulated, but are part of the 
stakeholder approach for fair business and sales practices. Complying with the legal requirements of protecting customer data 
and data security in general is an integral part of the processing of banking business for RBI.  The RBI Code of Conduct 
stipulates in writing that the RBI treats its customers with respect and does not discriminate against them. This is ensured 
through various initiatives and the provision of products and services across different channels. See also the chapter on 
Consumers and end-users  referring to social inclusion.102 Group  management report

title: Definition of value chain
heading: Definition of value chain
start_phrase: According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships and its supply chain.
summary:
- Explains how significant geographical markets and operating segments are defined for reporting, aligning with IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, the Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center segments are combined and presented as “Austria and other.”
- Provides employee headcount by geography as of 31/12/2024, covering only Group units with more than 100 employees. Regional totals include Central Europe 11,187, Southeastern Europe 12,455, Eastern Europe (Russia) 8,852, Ukraine 5,690, Austria 5,390, for a Group total of 43,574.
- Defines the value chain in line with ESRS, covering own operations plus upstream and downstream activities. Describes RBI’s business model: primarily deposit-taking and lending in Austria and CEE, with additional services in leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: funding sources (customer deposits, issued bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities; sustainability-related funding and liquidity risks are considered. Customer money in investment/pension funds is excluded from upstream. Suppliers of goods and services are included as part of upstream.
- Downstream value chain: on-balance sheet lending/leasing and financial investments that finance customers/investees and drive positive or negative sustainability outcomes. Corporate lending is the most material impact area, with retail lending also important. Lending to sovereigns/financial institutions and central bank investments (primarily for liquidity) are generally not key for sustainability reporting, though disclosed where market conventions (e.g., PCAF) exist. A second downstream key chain is assets under management in investment and pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without such control or look-through are excluded.
text:
Definition of value chain
According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and 
downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships and its supply chain. RBI’s business 
model is to provide banking services to corporate customers and retail customers in Austria and CEE. Although deposit and 
lending activities are the main focus of activity, RBI also offers leasing, asset management, pension fund business and 
investment banking services.

title: Description of the upstream value chain
heading: Description of the upstream value chain
start_phrase: The upstream value chain of RBI consists of the financial liabilities that are borrowed as deposits or issued as bonds or equity.
summary:
- Scope and segmentation: To enhance transparency, operating segments are defined using IFRS 8 thresholds. For the consolidated non-financial statement, the Group Corporates & Markets and Corporate Center segments are combined and reported as “Austria and other.”
- Significant geographical markets and workforce: Employee headcount as of 31/12/2024 totals 43,574 across Austria and CEE. Regional totals include Central Europe (11,187: Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia), Southeastern Europe (12,455: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, Romania, Serbia), Eastern Europe (8,852: Russia), plus Ukraine (5,690) and Austria (5,390). Figures cover Group units within the IFRS consolidation scope with more than 100 employees.
- Business model: RBI provides banking services to corporate and retail clients in Austria and CEE, focused on deposits and lending, and also offers leasing, asset management, pension fund business, and investment banking.
- ESRS-aligned value chain reporting: Information covers own operations and the upstream and downstream value chain, including products/services, business relationships, and supply chain.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises funding sources (deposits, bonds, equity) used to finance customer activities, with consideration of sustainability-related funding and liquidity risks. Customer investments in third-party investment and pension funds are excluded. Suppliers of goods and services for operations are also part of the upstream chain.
- Downstream value chain (financial assets): Primarily on-balance sheet lending and leasing activities. Corporate lending is the key value chain with greatest impact materiality; retail lending is an additional element. Lending to sovereigns and financial institutions and placements with central banks (mainly for liquidity) are not core to the sustainability-related value chain, though disclosed where market convention (e.g., PCAF) exists.
- Downstream value chain (assets under management): Includes investment and pension fund activities where RBI employees have direct operational control of the investment process. Third-party funds without such control or look-through capability are excluded.
text:
Description of the upstream value chain
The upstream value chain of RBI consists of the financial liabilities that are borrowed as deposits or issued as bonds or equity. 
These are a source of financing for RBI, which is used to fund the activities of customers. However, the funding and liquidity risk 
impact of sustainability matters on RBI’s own operations is taken into account. Money invested by customers in investment and 
pensions funds is not considered part of the upstream value chain. 
The suppliers of goods and services that RBI purchases in order to carry out operating activities are considered to be a further 
part of the upstream value chain.

title: Description of the downstream value chain
heading: Description of the downstream value chain
start_phrase: The main downstream key value chain of RBI consists of the on-balance sheet financial assets, which are lent or leased to customers and financial investment activities of RBI.
summary:
- Geographic segmentation and reporting: Operating segments are defined per IFRS 8; for the consolidated non-financial statement, “Group Corporates & Markets” and “Corporate Center” are combined as “Austria and other.”
- Workforce distribution: Headcount by geography as of 31/12/2024 totals 43,574, spanning Austria and CEE (Central, Southeastern, Eastern Europe, including Ukraine and Russia). Data covers IFRS-consolidated units with more than 100 employees.
- Value chain scope per ESRS: Reporting covers own operations and upstream/downstream value chains linked to RBI’s banking model (corporate and retail banking in Austria and CEE), plus leasing, asset management, pension funds, and investment banking.
- Upstream value chain: Comprises financial liabilities (deposits, bonds, equity) used to fund customer activities, with funding/liquidity sustainability risks considered; also includes suppliers of goods and services. Customer investments in investment/pension funds are excluded from upstream.
- Downstream value chain (material focus):
  - Primary: On-balance sheet financial assets (lending/leasing and investment activities), with corporate lending having the greatest sustainability impact materiality; retail lending is also key. Lending to sovereigns/financial institutions and central bank liquidity placements are not core to sustainability-related value chain, though disclosed where market practice (e.g., PCAF) exists.
  - Secondary: Assets under management in investment/pension funds where RBI has direct operational control; third-party funds without control/look-through are not key.
- Downstream activities deemed non-material/excluded: Cash and cash equivalents (mainly with central banks/financial institutions); trading assets/liabilities (short-term; climate market risk addressed under ESRS E1); non-consolidated associates and investees included only for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; investment property excluded (own-use property covered under in-house ecology for climate).
- Data maturity: 2024 value chain disclosures reflect available information; broader coverage expected as CSRD implementation advances.
- Stakeholder engagement (SBM-2): Key groups include shareholders/owners; customers (corporate, private, SME); employees and their representatives; regulators and supranational bodies (e.g., ECB, EIB, IFC, EBRD, MIGA, central banks); business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers); NGOs and civil society; membership organizations (e.g., WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI); the RBI Sustainability Council; and external ESG expert groups.
text:
Description of the downstream value chain
The main downstream key value chain of RBI consists of the on-balance sheet financial assets, which are lent or leased to 
customers and financial investment activities of RBI. These products are a source of financing for customers and investees in 
their activities, leading to positive or negative sustainability outcomes. Here the key value chain relates to lending to corporate 
customers; this value chain has the greatest impact materiality (impact materiality, inside-out). An additional key element of 
the sustainability-related value chain relates to lending to retail customers. Lending to sovereigns and financial institutions, or 
investments with central banks which are primarily for liquidity purposes, are not considered as an important element of the 
sustainability-related value chain. Nevertheless, where market convention has been established to include additional 
information on lending to sovereigns and financial institutions (e.g. Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials), information 
is provided.
A second downstream key value chain consists of assets under management in investment and pension funds. These products 
are a source of financing for investees in their activities, leading to positive or negative sustainability outcomes. Here only 
investment activity where RBI employees have direct operational control of the investment process is considered to be part of 
the value chain. This means third party funds, where there is no direct operational control of the investment process and the 
possibility to look-through to the underlying assets is limited, are not considered a key part of the value chain.Group management report 103
 ·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   The following activities in the downstream value chain activity, which RBI does not consider material, are not considered:
· Cash and cash equivalents, most of which is held at central banks or in other financial institutions.
· Exposure from trading assets and liabilities are not considered due to their short-term nature. However, 
sustainability risks for market risk are considered as part of own operations in ESRS E1: Climate change.
· Non-consolidated associates are considered for the purposes of Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions to the 
extent that in-house data is available. However, they are not considered for other aspects of the  value chain .
· Non-consolidated investees are considered for the purposes of Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions to the extent 
that in-house data is available. However, they are not considered for other aspects of the  value chain .
· Investment property is not included due to the non-core nature of the business. Nevertheless, own-use property and 
its impact on climate change is considered as part of the in-house ecology section in chapter Climate change .
Value chain information is currently provided in 2024 to the extent that RBI has ready access to the information. In future RBI 
expects to have access to more information as the CSRD develops.

title: General description of stakeholder engagement
heading: General description of stakeholder engagement
start_phrase: RBI defines its stakeholders as those people or groups of people that have a legitimate interest in the company through their direct or indirect business activities.
summary:
- Clarifies which downstream value chain elements are deemed immaterial and excluded: cash and cash equivalents; trading assets and liabilities (short-term; sustainability risks addressed under ESRS E1: Climate change); investment property (non-core). Own-use property impacts are covered in the Climate change chapter’s in-house ecology section.
- Non-consolidated associates and investees are considered only for Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions where in-house data exists; they are excluded from other value chain aspects.
- For 2024, value chain information is limited to data readily accessible to RBI, with broader coverage expected as CSRD implementation advances.
- Defines stakeholder engagement and identifies primary stakeholder groups: shareholders/owners; customers (corporate, retail, SMEs); employees and their representatives; regulatory and supranational bodies (e.g., ECB, central banks, MIGA, EIB, IFC, EBRD); business partners (consultants, auditors, suppliers); NGOs and civil society (including proxies for ecosystems, biodiversity, and local communities); industry and membership organizations (WKO, EACB, UNCG, UNEP FI); the RBI Sustainability Council; and external ESG expert groups.
- Emphasizes integrating stakeholder views and ESG expertise into governance and business practices.

title: Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
heading: Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
start_phrase: RBI engages with its stakeholders through various methods to ensure their interests and views are adequately considered in the company's strategy and business model.
summary:
- RBI engages stakeholders to incorporate their interests into strategy and business model, assess material sustainability topics, and refine sustainability management, while participating in national and international forums.
- Engagement formats and typical frequencies:
  - Conferences: annual/biannual events (e.g., sustainability summits, industry ESG forums).
  - Meetings: focused sessions with partners, regulators, and customers, often monthly/as needed.
  - Advisory sessions: quarterly or project-based with external ESG experts, partners, and internal stakeholders.
  - Training: regular, year-round education on ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, and sustainability strategies for employees, customers, and partners.
  - Formal committees: monthly/quarterly bodies (e.g., Sustainability Council, ESG Task Force, RBI Sustainability Committee, and workforce-related committees).
  - Working groups: cross-functional/internal-external teams on ESG initiatives, climate action, and reporting.
  - Written engagement: surveys (annual), newsletters (monthly), reports, correspondence, and transparent customer complaint channels.
- Key topics include ESG integration, sustainable finance, climate change, human rights, environmental impact, regulatory compliance, financial literacy, and sustainability performance.
- Organization: a decentralized engagement model where units (ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate Communications, Legal, Compliance, etc.) manage their own stakeholder interactions aligned to their expertise.
- Coordination: a central stakeholder dialogue database maintained by Group ESG & Sustainability consolidates inputs from all units for reporting, documentation, and monitoring.
text:
Frequency and formats of stakeholder engagement
RBI engages with its stakeholders through various methods to ensure their interests and views are adequately considered in 
the company's strategy and business model. The frequency of these engagements varies based on the needs and relevance of 
each stakeholder group. RBI uses various forms of communication with its stakeholders to evaluate the relevance of 
sustainability topics and uses the results to further develop its sustainability management. RBI also plays an active role in 
various national and international forums:
· C o n f e r e n c e s :   l a r g e  f o r m a l  g a t h e r i n g s  w h e r e  s t a k e h o l d e r s  c a n  d i s c u s s  a n d  s h a r e  i n f o r m a t i o n .  T h e s e  t y p i c a l l y  o c c u r  
annually or bi-annually. Examples include sustainability summits and industry conferences focused on topics such as 
sustainable finance, climate change and ESG integration.
· Meetings: smaller, more focused discussions with specific stakeholders, held as needed, often monthly. These 
meetings can involve business partners, regulatory authorities and customers, who discuss topics such as ESG 
requirements, financial literacy and sustainability initiatives.
· A d v i s o r y  s e s s i o n s :   s e s s i o n s  w h e r e  s t a k e h o l d e r s  p r o v i d e  a d v i c e  o r  i n p u t ,  i n c l u d i n g  o n e - o n - o n e  o r  g r o u p  d i s c u s s i o n s .  
These occur quarterly or as required for specific projects. Advisory sessions often involve external ESG experts, 
business partners and internal stakeholders, who address issues such as human rights, environmental impact and 
regulatory compliance.
· T r a i n i n g :   e d u c a t i o n a l  s e s s i o n s  a i m e d  a t  i n f o r m i n g  o r  d e v e l o p i n g  s t a k e h o l d e r s '  s k i l l s ,  s c h e d u l e d  r e g u l a r l y  t h r o u g h o u t  
the year. Training sessions cover a wide range of topics, including ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, and 
sustainability strategies for employees, customers and business partners.
