title: Organization of stakeholder engagement
heading: Organization of stakeholder engagement
start_phrase: RBI organizes its stakeholder engagement through a decentralized approach, where various units engage with stakeholders based on their specific areas of expertise and operational focus.
summary:
- Focus: How RBI engages stakeholders to inform strategy, business model, and sustainability management, and how these engagements are organized and tracked.
- Purpose: Gather stakeholder views, assess material sustainability topics (ESG, climate, human rights, compliance), and feed results into continuous sustainability improvement; active participation in national/international forums.
- Engagement formats and typical frequencies:
  - Conferences: large formal events (annual/biannual) on sustainable finance, climate change, ESG integration.
  - Meetings: targeted discussions (often monthly/as needed) with partners, regulators, customers on ESG requirements, financial literacy, sustainability initiatives.
  - Advisory sessions: one-on-one/group input (quarterly/as needed) with external ESG experts, partners, internal teams on human rights, environmental impact, regulatory compliance.
  - Training: regular programs year-round on ESG practices, financial literacy, compliance, sustainability strategies for employees, customers, partners.
  - Formal committees: monthly/quarterly bodies (e.g., Sustainability Council, Task Force on ESG, RBI Sustainability Committee, workforce-related committees) for decision-making on ESG and people topics.
  - Working groups: cross-functional and external collaborations on ESG projects, climate action, sustainability reporting.
  - Written engagement: surveys (annual), newsletters (monthly), reports, correspondence, and customer complaint channels to collect feedback and share updates on ESG, regulatory changes, performance.
- Organization model: Decentralized execution by specialized units (ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate Communications, Legal, Compliance), ensuring topic-relevant interactions.
- Governance and reporting: Central consolidation via a stakeholder dialogue database managed by Group ESG & Sustainability to document, monitor, and report engagement activities across the organization.
text:
Organization of stakeholder engagement
RBI organizes its stakeholder engagement through a decentralized approach, where various units engage with stakeholders 
based on their specific areas of expertise and operational focus. This model ensures that interactions are relevant and directly 
aligned with the specific topics and issues at hand. Each unit within RBI, including ESG & Sustainability Management, Corporate 
Communications, Legal and Compliance, is responsible for managing its own stakeholder interactions, tailored to the context 
of specific stakeholder groups.
While the execution of stakeholder engagement is decentralized, RBI maintains mechanisms, such as a stakeholder dialogue 
database organized by Group ESG & Sustainability, to collect and consolidate information from all units for reporting. This 
ensures effective documentation and monitoring of engagement activities across the organization.Group management report 105

text:
Purpose of stakeholder engagement
The purpose of RBI’s stakeholder engagement is to ensure that the interests and views of stakeholders are adequately 
considered in the company’s strategy and business model. Engaging with stakeholders allows RBI to:

Consideration of stakeholder engagement outcomes

title: Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
heading: Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
start_phrase: For RBI, understanding the interests and views of its key stakeholders is fundamental to aligning its strategy and business model with stakeholder expectations.
summary:
- Purpose of stakeholder engagement: to incorporate stakeholder interests into RBI’s strategy and business model by gathering insights, identifying material issues, advancing sustainability goals, enhancing transparency and accountability, and fostering collaboration and partnerships.

- Use of engagement outcomes: stakeholder feedback informs strategy and operations, shapes initiatives (sustainability, risk management, policies), supports decision-making with diverse perspectives, and is documented/reported where feasible to maintain transparency.

- 2024 engagement examples: advisory sessions with business partners on ESG risks, discussions on Modern Slavery Statement implementation, and employee/customer ESG surveys; these informed materiality assessments and the sustainability strategy.

- Due diligence and materiality assessment: structured engagement with shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, and NGOs via meetings, conferences, advisory sessions, and surveys; material topics selected per ESRS and guided by GRI and UN Global Compact; inputs from initiatives like UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and SBTi; continuous monitoring to track evolving stakeholder interests and trends.

- Governance for ESG: a Sustainability Council of external ESG experts guides strategy on economic, environmental, and social issues and anchors stakeholder concerns in policies.

- Climate and nature strategy: alignment with UNEP FI PRB; participation in international working groups (climate adaptation targets, biodiversity, pollution, human rights) and a core group shaping guidance to 2030; hosting a biodiversity day to raise awareness of nature’s economic interdependence; support for clients via tailored financial products and ongoing portfolio assessments.

- Circularity focus: event on circular economy (notably in packaging) to engage stakeholders and integrate circularity principles into business strategy; circularity identified as a key impact area under PRB commitments and target setting.
text:
Inclusion of stakeholders in due diligence and materiality assessment
For RBI, understanding the interests and views of its key stakeholders is fundamental to aligning its strategy and business 
model with stakeholder expectations. This understanding is fostered through a structured approach to due diligence and 
materiality assessments.
RBI actively engages with a diverse range of stakeholders, including shareholders, customers, employees, regulatory 
authorities, business partners and NGOs. This engagement occurs through various formats, such as meetings, conferences, 
advisory sessions and surveys. For instance, RBI conducted surveys with customers and employees in 2024 to assess their 
perspectives on ESG issues and held advisory sessions with business partners regarding ESG risks. The insights gathered from 
these interactions are integrated into RBI’s strategic objectives and operational adjustments, ensuring decisions are closely 
aligned with stakeholder expectations.
RBI conducts a comprehensive materiality assessment to identify and prioritize issues that are most relevant to both the 
company and its stakeholders. The selection of material topics is guided by the regulatory requirements of the European 
Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). Additionally, internationally recognized criteria and sustainability standards, such as 
the Global Reporting Initiative and the United Nations Global Compact, provide guidance.  This approach ensures RBI's strategy 
reflects the expectations of key stakeholders, including supervisory authorities and supranational organizations. 106 Group  management report
·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   RBI's longstanding experience in analyzing and identifying material topics supports and enhances the quality of the due 
diligence and materiality assessment process. Feedback mechanisms, such as surveys and workshops, along with evaluations 
of discussions held with individual stakeholder groups (customers, employees, rating agencies, NGOs and sustainability 
experts), are vital sources for understanding stakeholder interests. Notably, initiatives like the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible 
Banking and the Science Based Targets initiative play an important role in identifying areas where the greatest impact can be 
achieved, guiding strategic investment and focus.
To keep track of changes in stakeholder interests and emerging trends, RBI conducts an ongoing monitoring process. This 
proactive approach allows the company to adapt its strategy and business model as needed, ensuring continued alignment 
with stakeholder expectations and enhancing overall corporate resilience. This fosters stakeholder trust while simultaneously 
advancing value creation for the company and its investors.

title: Overall ESG strategy
heading: Overall ESG strategy

summary:
- RBI’s materiality and due diligence are strengthened by longstanding expertise and structured stakeholder engagement (surveys, workshops, and dialogues with customers, employees, rating agencies, NGOs, and sustainability experts).
- Global frameworks guide priorities: the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking serve as RBI’s core framework, complemented by participation in UNEP FI working groups and the Science Based Targets initiative to identify high-impact areas and direct strategic investment.
- Ongoing monitoring of stakeholder interests and emerging trends enables timely strategy and business model adaptations, building resilience, trust, and value creation.
- Recent stakeholder feedback validated RBI’s overall ESG strategy and business model, prompting no major changes while reinforcing integration of stakeholder insights into decisions.
- A Sustainability Council of external ESG and sustainability experts supports stakeholder dialogue and steers economic, environmental, and social policy direction.
- Climate and nature actions: RBI is the only DACH representative in an international UNEP FI core group shaping guidance to 2030; it participates in working groups on climate adaptation target setting, biodiversity, pollution, and human rights.
- RBI hosted a Biodiversity Day on 27 Nov 2024 with 100+ participants from finance, regulators, clients, and NGOs, emphasizing that over USD 44 trillion of global GDP depends on nature and translating this interdependence into actionable measures for industry and banking.

- Circularity is a key impact area under the PRBs; RBI organized a circular economy event (with focus on packaging) to advance sustainable practices, with insights feeding integration of circular principles into strategy and target-setting commitments.
text:
Overall ESG strategy
RBI continuously evaluates the interests and views of its stakeholders to ensure alignment with its strategy and business 
model. The most recent stakeholder feedback has largely confirmed the overall strategy and business model of the RBI and 
has not necessitated any significant changes. RBI remains committed to effectively integrating stakeholder insights into its 
decision-making processes.

title: Climate & nature
heading: Climate & nature
start_phrase: Since the UNEP FI´s principles for responsible banking serve as the guiding framework for RBI, RBI also participates in several UNEP FI working groups to foster its knowledge on practical implementation processes.
summary:
- RBI leverages its longstanding expertise to strengthen due diligence and materiality assessments, informed by structured stakeholder engagement (surveys, workshops, and dialogues with customers, employees, rating agencies, NGOs, and sustainability experts).
- External frameworks—including the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB) and the Science Based Targets initiative—guide impact identification, strategic focus, and investment priorities.
- Ongoing monitoring of stakeholder interests and emerging trends enables timely strategy and business model adjustments, reinforcing trust, resilience, and value creation.
- Recent stakeholder feedback confirmed RBI’s overall ESG strategy and business model; the bank remains committed to integrating stakeholder insights into decision-making.
- A Sustainability Council of external ESG experts advises on economic, environmental, and social priorities and supports stakeholder dialogue and sustainability management.
- Climate and nature: PRB serves as the guiding framework; RBI participates in UNEP FI working groups on climate adaptation target setting, biodiversity, pollution, and human rights, and acts as the sole DACH representative in a core group shaping guidance and potential 2030 requirements for signatory banks.
- RBI hosted a Biodiversity Day on 27 Nov 2024 with 100+ participants (including regulators, UN bodies, NGOs, and clients) to raise awareness of nature’s economic interdependence (USD 44 trillion of global GDP depends on nature) and highlight actionable measures for industry and banking.
- The bank’s strategy combines qualitative and quantitative criteria, offering tailored financial products to improve clients’ climate performance and conducting ongoing portfolio assessments to address sector-specific needs.
- Circularity: Recognizing its rising importance—especially in packaging—RBI convened a stakeholder event and is integrating circular economy principles into its strategy and operations; circularity is a designated PRB impact area supporting RBI’s target-setting commitments.
text:
Since the UNEP FI´s principles for responsible banking serve as the guiding framework for RBI, RBI also participates in several 
UNEP FI working groups to foster its knowledge on practical implementation processes.
· As the only DACH representative of banking groups, RBI is part of an international core group to assess how the 
world and the sustainable banking community have progressed, and to define common guidance and potentially 
requirements for signatory banks until 2030.
· RBI is participating in working groups on Climate Adaptation Target Setting, on biodiversity or pollution as well as on 
human rights.
On 27 November 2024, RBI hosted a biodiversity day, which focused on nature and biodiversity for the industry and banking 
sectors. It was a best practice event for raising awareness on nature & biodiversity and its interlinkage with the economy.The 
event attracted 100+ participants, including colleagues from the Raiffeisen sector, customers and representatives from various 
sectors, including the Austrian Financial Market Authority, UN Environmental Program for Financial Institutions, and 
international ESG experts, consultancies and NGOs. Biodiversity significantly impacts the economy, with over USD 44 trillion of 
global GDP dependent on nature. The event aimed to make this interdependence more tangible for clients and stakeholders, 
highlighting relevant measures for both industry and banking.
RBI's  strategy includes both qualitative and quantitative criteria to enhance its sustainability goals. This strategy supports 
customers and stakeholders in improving their climate performance through tailored financial products and involves ongoing 
assessments of the portfolio to adapt to sector-specific needs.

text:
Circularity
RBI recognizes the growing importance of circular economy practices, particularly within the packaging industry. To address 
this, RBI organized an event focused on circularity, bringing together various stakeholders to discuss and explore sustainable 
practices and the financial sector's role in promoting a circular economy. Insights gained from this event will inform RBI's 
ongoing efforts to integrate circular economy principles into its business strategy and operations, ensuring that stakeholder 
perspectives are continuously reflected in its approach to sustainability. Since committing to the UNEP FI Principles for 
Responsible Banking (PRBs), RBI has identified circularity as a key impact area. Events like these are crucial in helping RBI meet

heading: Human rights
start_phrase: T h e d e v e l o p m e n t o f R B I ' s G r o u p H u m a n R i g h t s P o l i c y i n 2 0 2 3 d e m o n s t r a t e s t h e c o m p a n y ’ s c o m m i t m e n t t o f o s t e r i n g d i a l o g u e o n h u m a n r i g h t s i s s u e s .

title: Next steps
heading: Next steps
start_phrase: RBI plans to continue its regular stakeholder engagements and materiality assessments to identify areas for potential improvement.
summary:
- Human rights: RBI developed a Group Human Rights Policy in 2023 through collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights and a cross-divisional working group; it is preparing a Modern Slavery Act statement with external consultants and legal experts; a cross-functional group met monthly in 2024 to integrate human rights due diligence into banking processes.
- Financial inclusion: In line with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, RBI hosted a Financial Inclusion Summit in Prague (Sept 2024) to share best practices, deepen work on financial education, products/services for vulnerable groups, and the EU Accessibility Act, with a UNEP FI keynote linking efforts to global expectations.
- Customer focus: Ongoing enhancements to complaint management and customer service, using continuous assessment of interactions and satisfaction to refine products and service strategies.
- Next steps: Continued stakeholder engagement and materiality assessments, monitoring and evaluating engagement effectiveness, and regular reviews of internal ESG policies to drive continuous improvement, trust, and transparency.
- Stakeholder engagement governance: Clear mechanisms to keep administrative, management, and supervisory bodies informed of stakeholder views (shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, NGOs, civil society, etc.), including systematic feedback from surveys/workshops/Sustainability Council, reporting NGO-raised controversies on human rights and climate/nature, and Sustainability Committee discussions that feed into strategic decisions by the Management and Supervisory Boards.
text:
Next steps
RBI plans to continue its regular stakeholder engagements and materiality assessments to identify areas for potential 
improvement. These ongoing efforts are essential for staying responsive to stakeholder needs and emerging trends, enabling 
the organization to adapt effectively within the evolving regulatory landscape.
RBI will monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of its stakeholder engagements and make necessary adjustments. Regular 
reviews of internal ESG policies ensure continuous improvement and alignment with best practices.
By continuously considering stakeholder feedback, RBI aims to strengthen its stakeholder relationships and ensure that their 
interests are adequately considered. This is expected to increase trust and transparency.

title: Stakeholder Engagement Governance
heading: Stakeholder Engagement Governance
start_phrase: RBI ensures that its administrative, management and supervisory bodies are informed about the views and interests of key stakeholders – including shareholders, customers, employees, regulatory and supranational authorities, business partners, NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, RBI membership organizations, the RBI Sustainability Council and external ESG expert groups – regarding sustainability-related impacts through several key mechanisms:
summary:
- Human rights: RBI developed a Group Human Rights Policy in 2023 through collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights and a cross-divisional working group, signaling a structured approach to expert- and stakeholder-informed strategy. RBI is preparing a Modern Slavery Act statement with external consultants and legal experts. In 2024, a cross-functional group met monthly to integrate human rights due diligence into banking processes.

- Financial inclusion and customer health: In line with UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, RBI prioritized financial inclusion, hosting a 2024 Prague summit that aligned Sustainability, Retail, and Marketing on best practices, financial education, services for vulnerable groups, and the upcoming EU Accessibility Act, with a UNEP FI keynote linking to global expectations. RBI is continuously refining complaint management and customer service based on feedback and satisfaction assessments.

- Next steps: Ongoing stakeholder engagement and materiality assessments will guide improvements. RBI will monitor the effectiveness of these engagements, adjust as needed, and regularly review internal ESG policies to strengthen relationships, trust, and transparency.

- Stakeholder engagement governance: Administrative, management, and supervisory bodies are kept informed of stakeholder views—from shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, business partners, NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, membership organizations, the Sustainability Council, and external ESG experts—via:
  - Regular engagement (surveys, workshops, Sustainability Council meetings), with insights and any NGO controversies on human rights or climate/nature reported to leadership.
  - Sustainability Committee discussions of materiality and feedback findings.
  - Regular updates on material impacts, ESG performance, risks, and compliance.
  - Internal communications (newsletter, intranet, monthly briefings).
  - A dedicated Group ESG & Sustainability Management team and local officers to run proactive dialogue and integrate insights into strategy.

- Own workforce engagement: Structured exchanges with the Works Council (including monthly jour fixe), Works Council meetings in Austrian subsidiaries, biennial employee engagement surveys, CEO calls with anonymous Q&A, and fireside chats and consultation hours with People, Culture & Organization.

- Workers in the value chain and affected communities: RBI factors customer practices and conditions for value chain workers and communities into due diligence and strategy. Participation in the UN Global Compact Human Rights Accelerator (2023) and PRB working groups (e.g., ILO Decent Work, best practice community), along with collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute, enhances due diligence for corporate customers. Ongoing supplier assessments and monitoring help prioritize and identify significant impacts.
text:
Stakeholder Engagement Governance
RBI ensures that its administrative, management and supervisory bodies are informed about the views and interests of key 
stakeholders – including shareholders, customers, employees, regulatory and supranational authorities, business partners, 
NGOs, civil society, employee representatives, RBI membership organizations, the RBI Sustainability Council and external ESG 
expert groups – regarding sustainability-related impacts through several key mechanisms:
· Regular stakeholder engagement: feedback from stakeholder engagement activities, such as customer satisfaction 
surveys, stakeholder workshops and meetings of RBI´s Sustainability Council, is systematically collected and 
presented to senior management. For example, insights gathered from a recent customer satisfaction survey are 
relayed to the Management Board to align strategies with customer expectations. Any controversy request on topics 
related to human rights or climate & nature which have been addressed to RBI by NGOs are reported to the 
management and supervisory body.

title: Stakeholder group: own workforce
heading: Stakeholder group: own workforce
start_phrase: RBI uses different formats to actively integrate the interests and views of its employees into its strategic framework.
summary:

- ESG organization: A Group ESG & Sustainability Management team acts as an internal ESG advisor, conducting proactive stakeholder dialogue and integrating feedback into sustainability strategy; local sustainability officers mirror this role in subsidiaries.
- Workforce engagement: Structured exchanges between management and the Works Council (including monthly meetings), regular Works Council meetings in Austrian subsidiaries, biennial employee engagement surveys, CEO video calls with anonymous Q&A, and fireside chats/consultation hours with People, Culture & Organization to discuss workforce topics.
- Value chain workers and affected communities: Participation in the UN Global Compact Human Rights Accelerator (2023) and PRB working groups (including ILO Decent Work and best-practice community) to strengthen human-rights due diligence for corporate customers. Collaboration with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights to establish the RBI Group Human Rights Policy. Ongoing supplier assessments and monitoring to set priorities and identify significant impacts.
- Outcome: These stakeholder formats feed insights to administrative, management, and supervisory bodies, enabling informed decision-making.

title: Stakeholder groups: workers in the value chain and affected communities
heading: Stakeholder groups: workers in the value chain and affected communities
start_phrase: It is of significance to RBI to considering customer practices and conditions in relation to value chain workers and affected communities.

- Internal communication: Tools such as a Sustainability Newsletter, the intranet, and monthly briefings keep employees informed about stakeholder views and ESG developments.
- ESG structure and roles: A Group ESG & Sustainability Management team serves as an internal advisor, leading proactive stakeholder dialogue and integrating feedback into sustainability strategies; local sustainability officers replicate this role in subsidiaries.

text:
Stakeholder groups: workers in the value chain and affected communities
It is of significance to RBI to considering customer practices and conditions in relation to value chain workers and affected 
communities. RBI has been part of the Human Rights Accelerator program of the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC) in 
2023 and actively participates in various PRB working groups focused on human rights, including the ILO Decent Work working 
group and the community on best practice. These dialogues have helped RBI enhance its due diligence processes for corporate 
customers, ensuring that the rights and interests of value chain workers and affected communities are incorporated into the 
overall strategy and decision-making processes of RBI.

title: Stakeholder group: consumer and end-user
heading: Stakeholder group: consumer and end-user
start_phrase: As a customer-centric organization, RBI puts the interests, views and rights of its customers and potential customers at the center of its strategy.
summary:
- Focus on the stakeholder group “consumer and end-user,” highlighting RBI’s customer-centric strategy aimed at becoming the most recommended financial services group through continuous innovation and superior customer experience.
- Integration of consumer insights into strategy via:
  - Code of Conduct ensuring respectful treatment, truthful marketing, and prioritization of consumer rights.
  - Commitment to responsible banking by signing the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
  - Multi-channel customer feedback mechanisms (surveys, digital interactions, in-branch surveys) informing product development and service.
  - Transparent, robust complaint management to enhance accountability and long-term relationships.
- Use of customer insights to design products and services that align with consumer interests and mitigate risks like over-indebtedness.
- Overview of SBM-3: identification and management of material impacts, risks, and opportunities within a complex economic, geopolitical, and environmental context.
- Explanation of the consolidated non-financial statement focusing on material sustainability topics reflecting stakeholder expectations and RBI’s impacts on economy, environment, and people (including human rights).
- Description of the 2024 double materiality assessment conducted per ESRS:
  - Impact materiality: RBI’s significant impacts on people and the environment.
  - Financial materiality: topics with actual or potential material financial effects on RBI.
  - Reference to IRO-1 for the process used to identify and assess material impacts, risks, and opportunities.
text:
Stakeholder group: consumer and end-user
As a customer-centric organization, RBI puts the interests, views and rights of its customers and potential customers at the 
center of its strategy. This is, embodied in its vision to become the most recommended financial services group and its mission 
to transform continuous innovation into superior customer experience. The integration of consumer insights into the strategy 
occurs through the following:
· Guidance from the Code of Conduct: the RBI Code of Conduct establishes standards for respectful treatment of 
customers and prohibits false or misleading marketing practices, ensuring that consumer rights and interests are 
prioritized in all interactions.
· Commitment to responsible banking: by signing the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking (PRBs), RBI has 
committed to responsible banking practices.
· Customer feedback mechanisms: RBI actively collects customer feedback from various sources, including 
satisfaction surveys, digital platform interactions and surveying customers directly in branches. This feedback is 
crucial for understanding customer needs and serves as an important information basis for product development 
and customer service.
· Transparent complaint management: RBI has set up a robust customer complaint management system with 
transparent channels for addressing feedback and concerns. This approach fosters accountability and enhances 
long-term relationships with customers.
The insights from customer feedback are incorporated into the development of products and services to ensure they align 
with consumer interests and to mitigate potential risks related to over-indebtedness and the handling of financial services.

title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with the strategy and business model - Introduction
heading: SBM- 3: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with the strategy and business model
start_phrase: As an internationally active banking group, RBI faces specific challenges in its efforts to realize its sustainability vision.
summary: Introduction to RBI’s approach to material impacts, risks, and opportunities: outlines the consolidated non-financial statement for FY2024, which focuses on sustainability topics deemed material through a double materiality assessment conducted in 2024 in line with ESRS. It addresses RBI’s specific impacts on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights), reflects stakeholder expectations, and distinguishes impact materiality (effects on people/environment) from financial materiality (current or future financial effects on RBI). The context notes numerous economic, geopolitical, and environmental risks, and refers readers to chapter IRO-1 for the assessment process.
text:
Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with the 
strategy and business model
As an internationally active banking group, RBI faces specific challenges in its efforts to realize its sustainability vision. These 
arise from the economic, social and environmental impacts of RBI’s business activities as well as from the external conditions 
within which it operates. RBI works within environment that is characterized by numerous economic, geopolitical and 
environmental risks. In the consolidated non-financial statement, it addresses the sustainability topics that have been 
identified within RBI as material, that reflect the expectations of its stakeholders, and that represented the focus of its 
engagement in 2024. This non-financial statement contains information describing the specific impact of RBI on the economy, 
environment and people, including human rights. The sustainability topics elaborated in the non-financial statement are the 
result of the double materiality assessment.
In financial year 2024, RBI performed a double materiality assessment based on the principles and requirements formulated in 
the ESRS. For an overview of how the assessment was performed, please refer to the chapter  IRO-1: Process to identify and 
assess material impacts, risks and opportunities . The assessment showed the topics through which RBI has been or is 
connected to a material impact on people or the environment (impact materiality) and the topics that now, or may in the 
future, have a material financial effect on RBI (financial materiality).110 Group  management report
·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024

title: Description of material impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: Description of material impacts, risks an d opportunities
start_phrase: The outcomes, including both the material topics from own operations as well as from the value chain, are shown below :
summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from RBI’s 2024 Group Management Report outlining double materiality findings and the management of sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) under ESRS.
- Core outcome: Most material issues are downstream in the lending and investment portfolios and assets under management; own operations and upstream suppliers are also assessed. Annual re-evaluation planned.
- Environmental (E):
  - E1 Climate change: Negative impacts from financing high‑carbon sectors; financial risks (credit, market, transition); opportunities in green financing, sustainability‑linked products, renewable/efficiency projects, and advisory. Own operations impacts across scopes 1–3; adaptation risks to buildings, asset lifespans, and energy/procurement prices; energy sourcing choices affect footprint.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Financing can drive biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation; alignment with UNEP FI PRB and regulatory expectations emphasized.
  - E5 Circular economy: Potential positives via procurement standards and efficient IT/hardware; downstream financing in real estate, transport, and energy contributes to waste and environmental strain.
- Social (S):
  - S1 Own workforce: DEI and inclusion benefits and risks (equal pay, discrimination, whistleblowing); employee development and training; health, safety, and well‑being; social dialogue and voice; secure employment, wages, work‑life balance; data privacy protection.
  - S2 Workers in the value chain: Potential human rights risks (forced/child labor, health and safety, wages, non‑discrimination) linked to financed clients and investments.
  - S3 Affected communities: Positive impacts via sector exclusions (tobacco, gambling, defense) and governance risk checks; social financings for essential services, jobs, and SME support (including women‑owned and underserved regions).
  - S4 Consumers/end-users: Privacy, cybersecurity, and resilience; responsible marketing and access to quality information; non‑discrimination; access to products and services. Identifies positive impacts, potential harms, and financial/regulatory risks.
- Governance (G1 Business conduct):
  - Culture of integrity and ethical compliance; whistleblower protection; anti‑corruption and bribery prevention/training; incidents risks; AML/CFT effectiveness; political engagement for informed policymaking; fair supplier relationships and ESG standards in procurement.
- Strategic linkages: Each topic mapped to business model responses (customer centricity, sustained growth, strong risk governance, efficiency), value chain segment (own operations, upstream, downstream), stakeholders, and time horizons.
- IRO management and methodology:
  - First ESRS‑aligned double materiality assessment conducted via workshops (Sep 2023–Jun 2024), separately for own operations and value chain, using ESRS 1 AR 16 touchpoints plus company‑specific topics.
  - Internal experts (compliance, data security, people & culture, facility management, procurement, risk, sustainable finance, subsidiaries, staff council, etc.) and ongoing external engagement (e.g., UNEP FI PRB working groups, ESG monitoring).
  - CSRD implementation team (finance and sustainability) led the process; subsidiaries perform aligned CSRD reporting.

title: Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities - Introduction
heading: IRO-1 : Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: In the consolidated non-financial statement, RBI addresses the sustainability topics that have been identified within RBI as material, that reflect the expectations of the stakeholders, and that represented the focus of its engagement.
summary: Overview of RBI’s ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment used to identify and assess material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs) forming the basis of the consolidated non-financial statement, covering current and potential positive/negative impacts from own operations and value chain, and related risks and opportunities arising from business activities and relationships. Describes the first assessment conducted via workshops from September 2023 to June 2024, performed separately for own operations and the value chain. Internal topic experts assessed direct impacts, while external stakeholder input was incorporated through ongoing channels, including participation in Principles for Responsible Banking working groups; ESG experts continuously monitor topic developments influencing materiality. The process is applied at group level by RBI and by EU subsidiary banks, which publish their own CSRD reports, with identification of ESRS touchpoints.
text:
Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
In the consolidated non-financial statement, RBI addresses the sustainability topics that have been identified within RBI as 
material, that reflect the expectations of the stakeholders, and that represented the focus of its engagement. 
The double materiality assessment process is used to identify and assess material Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities (IROs) 
based on the principle of double materiality, serving as the basis for the entire sustainability disclosure. This assessment 
ensures that the consolidated non-financial  statement covers all topics and sub-topics with the greatest current or potential 
positive and negative impacts related to RBI’s business activities, products, and services. This includes impacts directly 
attributable to RBI within its operations, as well as those to which it contributes through business relationships with other 
entities. Additionally, the risks and opportunities relevant to RBI in connection with these matters, or those that arise from its 
business activities or relationships, are also presented.
The first double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS was carried out and was conducted with the help of 
workshops in the period from September 2023 to June 2024. The double materiality assessment process was performed 
separately for own operations and the value chain . This process was used to separate the effects RBI has through its own bank 
operation s from the effects it has through its value chain.
For the  double materiality assessment, internal topic experts assessed direct impacts, identifying relevant impacts, risks, and 
opportunities within their areas of expertise. External stakeholders have been involved through various channels in RBI's 
materiality analysis for many years. As an example, RBI participates in national and international working groups, particularly 
Principle s for Responsible Banking (PRB) working groups,  to discuss material sustainability topics. ESG experts continuously 
monitor developments in ESG-related topics, which influence RBI’s materiality assessment. This procedure is conducted at both 
the group level by RBI and by EU subsidiary banks, which publish their own CSRD reports.
Identification of ESRS touchpoints

title: Own operations
heading: Own operations
start_phrase: The initial assessment for own operations was based on the list of potentially material topics according to ESRS 1 AR 16 data points and was expanded by adding company-specific topics.
summary:
- Focus: RBI’s process for identifying and assessing material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) for sustainability disclosure, aligned with ESRS and the double materiality principle.
- Scope of disclosure: Covers topics with significant positive/negative impacts from RBI’s operations, products, services, and value chain, and the related risks and opportunities to RBI.
- Methodology: A double materiality assessment conducted via workshops from September 2023 to June 2024, performed separately for own operations and the value chain.
- Stakeholder engagement: Internal topic experts evaluated direct impacts; external stakeholders engaged through ongoing channels such as PRB working groups; continuous ESG topic monitoring influences materiality.
- Organizational coverage: Assessment conducted at RBI Group level and by EU subsidiary banks, which publish their own CSRD reports.
- ESRS touchpoints for own operations: Initial topic set based on ESRS 1 AR 16 data points, expanded with company-specific issues, covering 10 topics (five environmental, four social, one governance) including sub-topics.
- Workshop process: Internal stakeholders were briefed on ESRS and double materiality, reviewed and refined the list of potentially material topics; topics without identified touchpoints were deemed not material and documented.
- Internal responsibilities: Materiality analysis driven by ESG-experienced stakeholders across functions including Compliance, Data Security/Risk/GDPR, Sustainable Finance, Procurement/Supply Chain, People & Culture, Facility Management, Risk Controlling, Corporate Citizenship, Marketing/Lobbying, Financial Inclusion/Literacy, Staff Council, and selected subsidiaries.
- Governance: The CSRD implementation project team, combining finance and sustainability experts, held primary responsibility for executing the double materiality assessment.
text:
Own operations
The initial assessment for own operations was based on the list of potentially material topics according to ESRS 1 AR 16  data 
points  and was expanded by adding company-specific topics. This included 10 topics (five environmental topics, four social 
topics, one governance topic), and the relevant sub-topics, as well as sub-sub-topics. In individual workshops, all internal 
stakeholders were  familiarized with ESRS and received an introduction to the double materiality assessment. The goal was to 
enable the experts to review the list and to adapt it based on their expert opinion. The list of relevant touchpoints  for RBI was 
presented, reviewed, and adapted if necessary by the internal stakeholders of RBI. In subsequent workshops, the list, already 
populated with suggestions from sustainability experts from RBI, was completed with potentially significant topics in 
collaboration with the relevant departments or completed with company-specific topics. If no touchpoint was identified, the 
topic was taken as not material for RBI and documented accordingly.
The internal stakeholders with ESG expertise from various departments are responsible for the topics mentioned below and 
conducted the materiality analysis :
· Compliance
· Corporate Citizenship / Donations, Corporate Volunteering
· Data Security / Risk Management  /GDPR
· Financial Inclusion / Literacy
· Group People, Culture and Organization
· In-house Ecology / Facility Management
· Lobbying / Political Engagement/Marketing
· Procurement / Supply Chain Management
· Risk Controlling
· Selected Subsidiaries
· Staff Council / Employee Representatives
· Sustainable Finance 
The main responsibility for the  double materiality assessment lay with the CSRD implementation project team, which is a 
cooperation of finance and sustainability experts .

title: Benchmark analysis
heading: Benchmark analysis
start_phrase: A benchmark analysis was also conducted, examining sustainability information (websites, non-financial statements) from nine European banks of comparable size regarding their engagement with these topics.
summary:
- Conducted a benchmark analysis of sustainability disclosures from nine similarly sized European banks to map touchpoints and identify sectoral impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Piloted AI in ESG decision-making using a language model to analyze public internal and external sources under the CSRD framework (RBI and five EU subsidiaries); combined AI with expert input to validate the internal double materiality assessment.
- Ran assessment workshops introducing the ESRS double materiality methodology, explaining evaluation criteria and scales for impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Applied a four-point severity scale (scale, scope, irremediability, probability) and a four-point likelihood scale across risks, opportunities, and potential impacts; treated potential human rights impacts as inherently likely per ESRS 1 para 48.
- Defined financial materiality as sustainability matters that cause or are expected to cause significant financial effects, considering resource continuity, relationship dependencies, and drivers of future value; set time horizons and assessed probabilities for risks and opportunities.
- Evaluated ESRS topics for positive/negative, actual/potential impacts, assessing origin (direct/indirect), location, time horizon, and then quantifying extent.
- Assessed portfolio impact materiality across the value chain using UNEP FI’s Impact Analysis Tool to evaluate indirect impacts aligned with ESRS.
- Segmented the portfolio by business line (non-retail, retail, assets under management) and profiled by NACE sector, country of operation, exposure at default, and booking country.
text:
Benchmark analysis
A benchmark analysis was also conducted, examining sustainability information (websites, non-financial statements) from nine 
European banks of comparable size regarding their engagement with these topics. The results of this research were 
documented to identify additional touchpoints and potential impacts, risks, and opportunities for the financial sector.

title: Artificial intelligence (AI)
heading: Artificial intelligence (AI)
start_phrase: As part of a pilot project, AI was integrated into the ESG decision-making processes.
summary:
- Conducted a benchmark analysis of sustainability disclosures from nine similarly sized European banks to map additional touchpoints and identify sector-specific impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Piloted AI to support ESG decision-making: a language model analyzed publicly available internal and external sources under the CSRD framework (RBI and five EU subsidiaries), combining AI outputs with expert validation to support RBI’s internal double materiality assessment.
- Ran assessment workshops introducing ESRS-aligned double materiality methodology, including:
  - Use of four-point scales (1–4) for severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood across risks, opportunities, and potential impacts.
  - Distinction between actual versus potential impacts; evaluation of origin (direct/indirect), location, time horizon, and quantitative extent.
  - Human rights treatment per ESRS 1 para. 48: potential human rights impacts considered without likelihood scoring and assumed likely for calculation.
- Financial materiality approach: a topic is financially material if it causes or is expected to cause significant financial effects, considering resource continuity, dependency on relationships, and other value drivers; risks/opportunities assessed with defined time horizons and probability of occurrence.
- Portfolio impact materiality assessment of the value chain conducted with the UNEP FI Impact Analysis Tool (aligned with PRB and ESRS) to evaluate indirect portfolio impacts.
- Portfolio segmentation for analysis by business line (non-retail, retail, assets under management), sector (NACE), country of operation, exposure at default (EAD), and booking country.
text:
As part of a pilot project, AI was integrated into the ESG decision-making processes. The pilot project included a language 
model-based analysis of external and internal information according to the CSRD framework, including reports from RBI and 
separate reports from the five subsidiary banks in the EU. Only publicly accessible documents and sources were included, 
utilizing general web sources. It was a hybrid approach, combining AI technologies with expert sustainability know-how. The 
results were used to validate RBI’s internal  double materiality assessment .

title: Assessment workshops
heading: Assessment workshops
start_phrase: In subsequent assessment workshops, the list with the touchpoints was completed with potentially significant topics in collaboration with the relevant departments or completed with company-specific matters.
summary:
- Benchmark analysis of sustainability disclosures from nine comparable European banks to identify additional touchpoints and sector-specific impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Pilot integration of AI into ESG decision-making aligned with the CSRD framework, using a language-model analysis of publicly available internal and external documents (RBI and five EU subsidiaries), combining AI outputs with expert sustainability knowledge to validate RBI’s internal double materiality assessment.
- Assessment workshops introducing the ESRS-based double materiality methodology, including evaluation criteria and scale construction; expansion of topic touchpoints with department input and company-specific matters.
- Materiality methodology:
  - Actual vs potential impacts assessed; origin (direct/indirect), location, and time horizon identified before quantitative scoring.
  - Severity measured via a four-step scale (very low to high) based on scale, scope, irremediability, and probability; likelihood also on a four-step scale for risks, opportunities, and potential impacts.
  - Human rights: potential impacts assessed like actual impacts per ESRS 1 para 48; likelihood not applied—topics involving human rights deemed likely for calculation.
  - Financial materiality determined by expected significant financial effects, considering resource use continuity, dependency on relationships, and other value drivers; time horizons defined and probabilities assessed for relevant risks and opportunities.
- Value chain impact materiality assessment performed with the UNEP FI Impact Analysis Tool (PRB-aligned) to evaluate indirect portfolio impacts against ESRS priorities.
- Portfolio segmented for analysis by business line (non-retail, retail, assets under management), industry sector (NACE), country of operation, exposure at default (EAD), and booking country.
text:
Assessment workshops
In subsequent assessment workshops, the list with the touchpoints was completed with potentially significant topics in 
collaboration with the relevant departments or completed with company-specific matters. At the beginning of the assessment 
workshops, the workshop participants were introduced to the double materiality analysis method according to ESRS. As part of 
this introduction, the evaluation methodology and the construction of the scales used to assess the impacts, risks, and 
opportunities of the topics were elaborated.
For actual negative impacts, materiality was based on the severity of the impact, while for potential negative impacts it was 
based on the severity and likelihood of the impact. For factors such as scale , scope, irremediability, and probability of 
occurrence, a four-step scale was used to measure the severity of the impact, ranging from one (very low) to four (high). The 
likelihood of occurrence of a sustainable topic was also assessed for risks, opportunities, and potential impact using a four-
step scale, from one (very unlikely) to four (likely). The same likelihood scale was used for the probability of occurrence for 
financial materiality and impact materiality. For potential impacts on human rights, the assessment was conducted in the 
same manner as for actual impacts, in accordance with ESRS 1 paragraph 48. The likelihood was not applied by the potential 
impact on human rights, and if human rights were relevant to the topic, they were automatically considered likely for 
calculation purposes.
For the financial risks and opportunities assessment, a sustainability matter is considered material from a financial perspective 
if it triggers or is expected to trigger significant financial effects on the undertaking. This determination used factors such as 
the continuation of resource use, dependence on relationships, and other elements that influence the future value of the 
company. For risks and opportunities deemed relevant to RBI, the time horizon for potential occurrences was defined before 
analyzing how these risks and opportunities could impact the factors used. Additionally, the probability of occurrence was 
assessed.
During the workshops, the identified ESRS topics were subsequently evaluated for their positive and negative effects, and for 
each impact, additionally assessed for potential and actual impacts. Actual impacts are those that have already occurred, 
while potential impacts are those that could occur in the future. Initially, the origin of the impact (whether directly or indirectly 
caused by RBI), the location (where the expected impact could occur), and the time horizon in which the impacts are likely to 
occur were assessed. Subsequently, a quantitative evaluation was conducted to determine the extent.

heading: Impact materiality assessment
start_phrase: The portfolio’s impact materiality assessment was conducted using the United Nations Environment Programme – Finance Initiative (UNEP FI) Impact Analysis Tool.
summary: The partial document outlines RBI’s double materiality approach under ESRS/CSRD, starting with a benchmark of nine similarly sized European banks to identify touchpoints and sectoral impacts, risks, and opportunities. It details a pilot use of AI—language-model analysis of public internal/external sources across RBI and five EU subsidiaries—combined with expert input to validate RBI’s double materiality assessment. Assessment workshops introduced ESRS methods and scoring, applying four-level scales for severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood, distinguishing actual vs. potential impacts, and treating potential human rights impacts as automatically likely per ESRS 1. Financial risks and opportunities were assessed by likelihood and magnitude over defined time horizons, with magnitude linked to downstream income dependency. For portfolio impact materiality, RBI used UNEP FI’s Impact Analysis Tool, segmenting portfolios (non-retail, retail, AUM) by sector (NACE), geography, and EAD, mapping sector/geography to ESRS sub-topics, focusing on direct impacts. Impact scores combine scale (EAD), scope (country needs), and irremediability, with a 66.7% threshold for materiality and room for qualitative adjustment. Financial materiality of value-chain risks is confirmed when the topical income dependency exceeds 10% and impact is likely; the ratio is defined as income from high-impact lending/investing over operating income plus interest and fee add-backs, with components specified (interest and fee income from NFCs, mortgages, investment/pension funds). Currently, climate change (E1) is financially material for risks, and opportunities in E1 and S3 (affected communities) are deemed financially material. The validation phase cross-checked results against GRI Financial Services and SASB financial sector standards.
text:
Impact materiality assessment  
The portfolio’s impact materiality assessment was conducted using the United Nations Environment Programme – Finance 
Initiative (UNEP FI) Impact Analysis Tool. This tool, developed in collaboration with signatories of the Principles for Responsible 
Banking (PRB) and UNEP FI member banks, provides a framework for assessing the impacts associated with financial portfolios. 
By using this methodology, RBI evaluates the indirect impacts of its portfolio on sustainability priorities aligned with the 
European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).
For the analysis, RBI’s portfolio was segmented by business line — non-retail, retail, and assets under management — and 
described in terms of industry sectors (NACE), country of operation, exposure at default (EAD), and booking country.Group management report                                                                                                                                                    117
 ·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   To assess how these portfolio elements impact sustainability topics, UNEP FI mappings are used to connect sector and 
geographic data to ESRS sub-topics. The sector-impact map highlights how industries influence specific impact areas — 
positively or negatively, directly or indirectly — and these impact areas are then mapped to ESRS sub-topics to connect 
portfolio impacts to ESRS standards. Adding country-specific needs data gives the analysis a geographic layer, helping to 
prioritize sustainability topics based on regional importance. While the ESRS standards require reflection on both actual and 
potential impacts, which could align with UNEP FI’s direct and indirect impacts, RBI’s analysis focuses solely on direct impacts. 
This decision provides a clearer view of the immediate effects of the portfolio, while the overall analysis remains within the 
ESRS indirect realm from RBI’s perspective.
The impact calculation applies three measures: scale, scope, and irremediability. Scale quantifies the monetary exposure (EAD) 
of sectors that directly affect ESRS sub-topics through UNEP FI impact areas. Scope adjusts scale by factoring in geographic 
relevance, reflecting country-specific needs that influence the priority of each topic. Irremediability then provides a qualitative 
assessment of the reversibility or permanence of these impacts, with higher scores indicating sectors or regions where impacts 
are challenging to mitigate.
These three measures — scale, scope, and irremediability — combine to create an overall impact score for each ESRS sub-topic. 
This score serves as the basis for the double materiality analysis, following ESRS guidelines. A materiality threshold of two-
thirds (66.7 per cent) is applied to determine which ESRS topics are considered material and should be prioritized. The 
quantitative score can also be adjusted using qualitative inputs such as stakeholder feedback or contextual insights, ensuring 
a more holistic assessment of the portfolio’s indirect impacts.

title: Financial materiality from risks in the value chain
heading: Financial materiality from risks in the value chain
start_phrase: According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships, and its supply chain.
summary:
- Uses UNEP FI sector and geographic mappings to link portfolio exposures to ESRS sub-topics, focusing on direct impacts to clarify immediate portfolio effects while acknowledging the ESRS indirect impact perspective.
- Applies a three-part impact methodology:
  - Scale: monetary exposure (EAD) of sectors affecting ESRS sub-topics.
  - Scope: adjusts for country-specific needs to reflect geographic relevance.
  - Irremediability: qualitative assessment of reversibility/permanence of impacts.
- Combines these measures into an overall impact score per ESRS sub-topic, applies a 66.7% materiality threshold, and allows qualitative adjustments (e.g., stakeholder input) for a holistic view.
- Assesses financial materiality of risks across own operations and the value chain based on likelihood (legislation, reputation) and magnitude via income dependency of the downstream value chain.
- Defines income dependency ratio as income from high-impact lending/investing divided by operating income plus add-back of interest and fee expenses; considers >10% plus likely impact as confirming financial materiality.
- Specifies income sources counted as high-impact: interest from non-financial corporations, retail mortgages; fees/commissions from non-financial corporations and investment/pension funds.
- Concludes that financial materiality in the value chain currently applies to ESRS E1 Climate change.
- Identifies financially material opportunities in E1 Climate change and S3 Affected communities, emphasizing integration of sustainable business into core operations.
- Validates the double materiality assessment by benchmarking preliminary results against GRI Financial Services Sector Standard and SASB standards (asset management & custody, commercial banks, consumer finance, mortgage finance).
- Context: Part of RBI’s CSRD implementation and Group management report for Financial Year 2024.
text:
Financial materiality from risks in the value chain
According to ESRS, it is necessary to report information related to an undertaking’s own operations and its upstream and 
downstream value chain, including its products and services, its business relationships, and its supply chain. The financial 
materiality of risks is assessed based on a combination of the likelihood of occurrence and the potential magnitude of the 
financial effects. For the likelihood of occurrence, factors such as current and future legislation as well as reputational 
considerations are considered. For the purpose of the CSRD, RBI uses the income dependency of RBI’s downstream value chain 
to assess the magnitude of the financial materiality of the topical standards and sub-topics.
When the income dependency of a topical standard is greater than ten per cent and it is likely there will be an impact, this 
provides confirmation of financial materiality. The income dependency ratio is defined as (income from high-impact lending/
investing) divided by (operating income and add-back interest expense and fee expense). 
The income from high-impact lending/investing currently consists of the following positions:
· Interest income from non-financial corporations
· Interest income from retail mortgage loans
· Fee and commission income from non-financial corporations
· Fee and commission income from investment funds/pension funds
Financial materiality  in the value chain  currently applies to climate change (E1).

Financial materiality from opportunities in the value chain
Based on the importance of sustainable business within the ESRS standard  E1 – Climate change and S3 – Affected 
communities, it can be seen that business opportunities are identified as financially material for RBI. Therefore, it is imperative 
for RBI to integrate sustainable business practices into its core operations, as this not only mitigates risks but also presents 
business opportunities.

title: Validation of double materiality assessment
heading: Validation of double materiality assessment
start_phrase: At the beginning of the validation process, the preliminary results were compared by the CSRD implementation project team against sector-specific criteria outlined in the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB).
summary:
- The document outlines a methodology that maps portfolio sectors and geographies to ESRS sub-topics using UNEP FI sector-impact and country-needs mappings. It prioritizes direct impacts for clarity, while acknowledging ESRS’s focus on both actual and potential (direct and indirect) impacts, and frames the overall analysis as indirect from RBI’s perspective.
- Impact scoring combines three measures: scale (EAD exposure linked to ESRS sub-topics via UNEP FI impact areas), scope (geographic relevance based on country needs), and irremediability (difficulty of reversing impacts). These produce an overall score per ESRS sub-topic.
- A materiality threshold of 66.7% determines which ESRS topics are material; scores can be adjusted with qualitative inputs such as stakeholder feedback for a more holistic view.
- Financial materiality of risks in the value chain is assessed via likelihood (legislation, reputation) and magnitude, with magnitude proxied by income dependency on high-impact lending/investing. The defined income dependency ratio uses interest and fee income from non-financial corporates, retail mortgages, and investment/pension funds; currently, financial materiality applies to ESRS E1 Climate change.
- Business opportunities linked to ESRS E1 Climate change and S3 Affected communities are deemed financially material, reinforcing the need to integrate sustainable practices into core operations.
- Validation compared preliminary results with GRI and SASB financial sector standards. An overall 0.66 threshold was set for both impact and financial materiality; topics exceeding it are included in the 2024 consolidated non-financial statement. Results were presented and recognized by governance bodies (Management Board and Audit Committee) with specified dates and summarized in SBM-3.
- Topic-specific disclosure on Climate change (own operations): impact materiality focuses on absolute scope 1–3 GHG emissions from energy use and business travel, recognizing global impacts without regional limits. While financed emissions are larger, own-operations impacts and mitigation (renewables, energy efficiency) are considered.
- Financial materiality for own operations covers physical, regulatory, and reputational risks. Physical risks (e.g., natural disasters, increased cooling needs) are mitigated via site selection, insurance, continuous monitoring, and energy-efficiency measures. Risks are material if they threaten medium- to long-term climate targets or are flagged by stakeholders; risk management combines top-down and bottom-up approaches.
- RBI aligns with the Paris Agreement by reducing emissions and supporting renewables. Using SBTi methodology, group targets for own operations were recalculated to a 1.5°C pathway, with 2024 set as the new base year due to scope expansion and more data points.
- Operational opportunities include KPI-driven steering of business travel and energy use, reputational benefits, increased resilience, and collaboration and investment in energy efficiency to support the broader transition to a sustainable economy.
text:
Validation of double materiality assessment
At the beginning of the validation process, the preliminary results were compared by the CSRD implementation project team 
against sector-specific criteria outlined in the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the Sustainability Accounting Standards 
Board (SASB). This involved examining the Financial Services Sector Standard by GRI and the financial sector standards provided 
by SASB, which encompassed asset management & custody activities, commercial banks, consumer finance, and mortgage 
finance.

·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   The result of the double materiality assessment was presented by the operational Steering Committee headed by the CFO . In 
addition to decisions for some entity-specific open issues, an overall threshold of 0.66 was set for the impact materiality and 
financial materiality (risks and opportunities), derived from assessments of various criteria. If the impact materiality and/or 
financial materiality of an ESRS topic exceeded this threshold, it was considered material for RBI and was included in the 
consolidated non-financial statement for 2024.
The process and the results of the direct double materiality assessment  were presented together with the indirect double 
materiality assessment (see point 2.2.) and recognized by the Management Board in a meeting on 23 January 2024 and by the 
Audit Committee of the Supervisory Board on 20 February 2024. A further update to the  Management Board  was made on 16

title: Impact materiality assessment
heading: Impact materiality assessment
start_phrase: In terms of RBI’s own operations, the double materiality principle means understanding and taking into account the impact of a company’s own activities on the environment and the impacts of environmental issues for the respective company.
summary:
- Governance and thresholds: The CFO-led operational Steering Committee presented the double materiality assessment, setting a uniform threshold of 0.66 for both impact and financial materiality; ESRS topics exceeding this were deemed material and included in RBI’s 2024 consolidated non-financial statement.
- Oversight and approvals: Direct and indirect double materiality assessments were presented and acknowledged by the Management Board (23 Jan 2024) and the Audit Committee (20 Feb 2024), with a further Management Board update on 16 Apr 2024; results are summarized in SBM-3.
- Topic-specific focus: Climate change—Own operations.
- Impact materiality (inside-out): Emphasis on absolute GHG emissions (Scopes 1–3) from energy use and business travel; negative climate impacts are recognized without regional limitation; mitigation through renewable energy and energy efficiency, with acknowledgment that financed emissions are larger but own operations remain material.
- Financial materiality (outside-in): Identification of physical, regulatory, and reputational risks linked to climate change and companies’ inaction; examples include natural disasters affecting assets, managed via location choices and insurance as part of adaptation.
- Risk management approach: Continuous monitoring, specialist input, and a combined bottom-up/top-down model; risks are material if they threaten medium- to long-term climate targets (notably energy consumption) or are flagged by stakeholders; measures include energy efficiency upgrades and building improvements.
- Costs and resilience: Anticipation of higher operating costs from physical climate impacts (e.g., cooling needs) and actions to enhance resilience and reduce reputational risk.
- Targets and methodologies: Use of SBTi methodology in 2024 to recalibrate own-operations targets aligned with a 1.5°C pathway under CSRD; 2024 set as the new base year due to expanded consolidation scope and more comprehensive CO2 data.
- Opportunities: KPI-driven steering of business travel and energy use, support for renewable energy, R&D collaborations, and investments in energy efficiency to aid the broader sustainability transition.
text:
Impact materiality assessment  
In terms of RBI’s own operations, the double materiality principle means understanding and taking into account the impact of a 
company’s own activities on the environment and the impacts of environmental issues for the respective company.
At RBI, the key materiality indicator is the volume of absolute greenhouse gas emissions (scopes 1-3) that are caused by various 
activities, such as energy consumption and business trips. These emissions have an adverse impact on the climate and are 
therefore considered, even though the main focus rests on RBI’s financed emissions due to their much larger weight. As the 
changes in the world’s climate have far-reaching consequences which extend beyond national borders, there is no regional 
limitation of effects in the context of the inside-out approach. Although the impact of greenhouse gas emissions on the 
climate is entirely negative, aspects such as the use of renewable energy and the promotion of energy efficiency can mitigate 
the adverse effects.

title: Financial materiality assessment
heading: Financial materiality assessment
start_phrase: The risks of operational activities are closely related to the environmental concerns set out to be managed in the CSRD.
summary:
- Governance and thresholding of double materiality: An operational Steering Committee led by the CFO set a unified threshold of 0.66 for impact and financial materiality. ESRS topics exceeding this level are deemed material and included in the 2024 consolidated non-financial statement. The process and results (direct and indirect assessments) were presented to and recognized by the Management Board (Jan 23, 2024), the Audit Committee (Feb 20, 2024), with a further update on Apr 16, 2024. Outcomes are summarized in SBM-3.

- Climate change – own operations:
  - Impact materiality: Primary indicator is absolute GHG emissions (Scopes 1–3) from activities like energy use and business travel. While financed emissions are larger and prioritized, own-operations impacts are globally relevant with no regional limitation. Mitigation includes renewable energy adoption and energy efficiency.
  - Financial materiality: Outside-in risks include physical, regulatory, and reputational dimensions. Physical risks (e.g., natural disasters, higher cooling needs) are mitigated via site selection, insurance, and efficiency measures. Risks are material if they threaten medium- to long-term climate targets (notably energy) or stakeholders deem them material. Management uses continuous monitoring, specialist input, and a combined bottom-up/top-down approach. Opportunities include KPI-based steering (travel, energy), stronger resilience, reputational benefits, R&D collaborations, and efficiency investments.
  - Targets and alignment: RBI contributes to Paris Agreement goals; in 2024 it recalculated group operational targets using the SBTi methodology to align with a 1.5°C pathway under CSRD. 2024 is the new base year due to expanded scope and improved data coverage.

- Value chain and risk assessment framework:
  - Complement to portfolio impact analysis: Alongside the UNEP FI tool (inside-out), RBI implemented an annual outside-in climate and environmental risk assessment per ECB guidance to gauge severity across time horizons via transmission channels.
  - Multi-dimensional assessment covers: (1) risk drivers (physical, transition, other environmental), (2) transmission across risk types (credit, market, operational, liquidity), and (3) impacts under multiple transition scenarios (linked to climate stress testing).

- Transition risk and transmission channels (per BCBS):
  - Credit risk: For corporates, scenario inputs (carbon tax, ETS costs) feed sector forecasts and borrower financials to project PDs; for retail, higher energy costs and inflation increase burdens. Materiality reflects lower profitability, asset devaluations, and reduced household wealth.
  - Market risk: Policy, technology, and sentiment shifts can reprice assets and increase volatility; commodity markets—especially fossil fuels—are exposed. Correlation breakdowns may weaken hedging effectiveness.
text:
Financial materiality assessment
The risks of operational activities are closely related to the environmental concerns set out to be managed in the CSRD. The 
biggest risk to the economy, society and the environment is the unwillingness of companies to counteract climate change 
which leads to increased global warming with the known negative impacts. In addition to external environmental risk, RBI and 
its operating locations are subject to physical, regulatory and reputational risks (outside-in perspective). In the area of physical 
risks, for example, natural disasters could result in damage to property. These risks are minimized by selecting the right 
locations and ensuring suitable property insurance (adaptation strategy).
These risks are managed by continuously observing the internal and external environment and by consulting specialists in 
controlling the respective measures. Risks are classified as material when they endanger the achievement of RBI’s medium to 
long-term climate targets – particularly with regard to energy consumption – or when stakeholders classify them as material 
for RBI. The measures set out are currently heavily focused on the area of energy, with examples including targeted increases 
in energy efficiency and structural alterations to building shells.
The physical risks of climate change, such as greater and more frequent temperature fluctuations, often result in higher 
operating costs, e.g. due to the increased need for cooling. Risk management is based on a combined bottom-up and top-
down approach in which all employees also play a significant role in risk minimization in their respective working area.
RBI is making a positive contribution to society with concrete steps relating to environmental management. RBI is contributing 
to meeting the goals of the UN climate change conference in Paris (Conference of the Parties 21) by working to reduce 
greenhouse gas emissions, as well as promoting the renewable energy sector of the economy.  In 2024, the methodology 
provided by SBTi was used to recalculate the group targets  for its own operations to align with the 1.5°C pathway required by 
the CSRD.  Due to the expanding consolidation scope as well as an increasing number of data points considered for the CO 2 
footprint, 2024 was set as the new base year to calculate RBI’s new emission reduction targets.
Consistent steering through KPIs in areas such as business travel and energy consumption represents a particular opportunity 
for RBI with regard to the environmental impact of its own operations. Furthermore, reputational risks are minimized and 
resilience in the face of the consequences of climate change is increased. New collaborations in research and development and 
investment in energy efficiency measures can also play a role in promoting the transformation to a sustainable economy.Group management report                                                                                                                                                    119

start_phrase: To complement the impact analysis performed using the UNEP FI Portfolio Impact Analysis Tool (s ee chapter Impact materiality assessment and in line with the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks (expectations 7.2 and 7.31), an extended annual risk assessment for climate and environmental risk drivers has been implemented within RBI’s risk framework.

The assessment adopts an outside-in perspective to gauge how climate and environmental risks affect RBI’s risk profile, while noting that inside-out aspects (e.g., financed emissions and science-based targets) are covered elsewhere.
