title: E1-9: Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities - Introduction
heading: 20.8 E1-9 : Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-rela ted opportunities
start_phrase: The assessment of the material risk positions with physical risk based on the European Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 of 30 November 2022 amending the implementing technical standards laid down in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/637 as regards the disclosure of environmental, social and governance risks - Template 5: Banking book - Climate change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk were prepared taking into account the IFRS scope of consolidation.
summary: RBI outlines its climate physical risk disclosure for the banking book under EU Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 amending 2021/637 (Template 5), using the IFRS scope of consolidation and relying on counterparties, third-party vendors, and public registers, with a liability disclaimer and noted data limitations (incomplete/unenforced Energy Performance Certificates in CEE, proxy use of registration/headquarter addresses for non-financial corporations, incomplete geographic coverage, internal data quality issues, and vendor threshold calibration volatility). Two tables segment exposures by region and assess physical risk at counterparty address for selected NACE sectors (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, L) and at collateral address for commercial/residential real estate exposures, with time horizons aligned to ICAAP (short ≤3 years, medium ≤10, long >10) based on remaining maturity, and splits by acute vs chronic risk and climate change adaptation alignment. For non-financial corporations in scope, €12,124 million (33.9%) is subject to physical risk, comprising €2,930 million chronic-only, €7,807 million acute-only, and €1,387 million both, with €0 million identified as covered by climate change adaptation actions; a regional table provides detailed proportions and maturity breakdowns.
text:
E1-9 : Anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and 
potential climate-rela ted opportunities
The assessment of the material risk positions with physical risk  based on the European Commission Implementing Regulation 
(EU) 2022/2453 of 30 November 2022 amending the implementing technical standards laid down in Implementing Regulation 
(EU) 2021/637 as regards the disclosure of environmental, social and governance risks  - Template 5: Banking book - Climate 
change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk were prepared taking into account the IFRS scope of consolidation. 
In assessing a counterparty’s ESG data, RBI relied on the completeness and correctness of data and documents received from 
such counterparty and, where applicable, third-party vendors and public registers. Assessments regarding the fulfillment of 
technical criteria were also based on details and information provided by the counterparty, which could not be fully verified. RBI 
does not assume liability for the correctness and completeness of underlying data as submitted by counterparties, and, where 
applicable, by third-party vendors and public registers.
With regard to energy efficiency information, multiple difficulties were encountered that explain different fill grades among 
the CEE countries. The main drivers of lacking data were: Energy Performance Certificates (EPC) had not been established in 
the local legislative; EPCs existed but had not been enforced by local law.
Another challenge with respect to data collection involved the physical risk assessment. First of all, for  non-financial 
corporations , the registration address and headquarter address of counterparties were partly used as a proxy location for the 
physical risk assessment. Furthermore, internal data quality and incomplete geographical coverage by RBI’s data provider did  
334                                                                                                                                                   Group management report 
·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   
not allow a physical risk assessment for the entire portfolio in scope. Also, calibration of thresholds provided in collaboration 
with the vendor may have resulted in volatility in physical risks.
In view of the challenges outlined above, the disclosure  has been made on the basis of currently available information, RBI’s 
best understanding of the regulatory requirements, as well as banking diligence. Due to deficiencies in data quality, lack of 
precise methodological guidance, and absence of widely shared and aligned practices, the interpretation of the results i s 
subject to limitations and is expected to develop over the next years.
The tables below segment the exposures per geographical region and provide a breakdown of those exposures subject to 
physical risk on a regional level, between those subject to acute or chronic risk only, or both acute and chronic risks 
simultaneously. In addition, a part of the exposure subject to physical risk that was identified as aligned with the climate 
change adaptation climate goal is shown. An additional split was made between the two tables, with the first one being 
populated based on the physical risk assessment performed at the level of the counterparty’s address with a focus on specific 
NACE sectors within the non-financial corporations portfolio. The second table was populated based on the physical risk 
assessment performed at the level of the collateral’s address, with a focus on commercial and residential real estate 
collateralized exposures within non-financial corporations and households portfolios. Definitions of the short  (up to three 
years), medium (up to ten years), and long-term (above ten years) time horizons  in the tables were aligned with internal ICAAP 
definitions . Exposures were grouped into the mentioned tenor groups based on the remaining maturity of the outstanding 
loans. 
Out of the total exposure from non-financial corporations under the scope of the assessme nt, € 12,124  million, or 33.9 per cent, 
was identified as subject to physical risk, of which €  2,930  million was sensitive to chronic risks only,  € 7,807  million was 
sensitive to acute risks only, and € 1,387  million was sensitive to both chronic and acute physical risks. Out of the total exposure 
sensitive to physical risk, € 0 million was covered by climate change adaptation actions (assessed as environmentally

Biodiversity and eco systems
E4-2: Policies related to biodiversity and ecosystems
Value chain
Due to the impact on a bank’s risk assessment, environmental topics such as biodiversity are covered in RBI’s risk framework 
(see chapter GOV-5: Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting ). Furthermore, RBI has developed a 
policy (RBI Group Biodiversity Policy) related to biodiversity and ecosystems during the financial year and plans to publish it in 
2025. The following topics will be addressed in the policy: 
· Definitions 
· Exclusion list 
· Materiality assessment results and proposed mitigation actions 
· Next steps and expected timeline 
The policy is consolidated by Group  Financial Institutions, Country & Portfolio Risk Management in coordination with the 
respective business lines as well as with Group ESG & Sustainability Management. This is to ensure harmonization with legal 
requirements as well as with voluntary commitments such as the PRBs. The implementation is scheduled for 2025 and will be 
carried out by the respective business units, with oversight from Group Financial Institutions and Country & Portfolio Risk 
Management.
RBI acknowledges and seeks alignment with internationally acclaimed standards, such as the Nature Target Setting 
Framework. This framework is in line with the missions of the Global Biodiversity Framework, the Taskforce on Nature-related 
Financial Disclosures (TNFD), Science Based Targets Networ k (SBTN) and leading net zero frameworks.
Policies for assets under management
Policy on biodiversity 
Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. fulfills its responsibility towards major stakeholders, such as customers, issuers or 
partner organizations, amongst others, by making a suitable contribution towards fighting the nature crisis, which has far-
reaching consequences for the environment, the economy and society. As a financial market participant, Raiffeisen 
Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H. also actively supports the necessary transformation towards a more sustainable value 
chain. The following essential components are part of the policy:
· Collaboration and knowledge transfer
· Engagement with companies
· Impact analysis (investment portfolio)
· Setting targets and disclosure
Biodiversity and natural capital are complex topics that are difficult to quantify. A universal metric is currently not possible and 
geospecific data is often incomplete, leading to estimates. International frameworks and reporting standards are evolving, and 
the strategy will be adjusted in the event of significant changes.
The implementation and monitoring of the policy are the responsibility of the Chief Sustainability Investment Officer (CSIO) at 
the executive management level.Group management report                                                                                                                                                    337
 ·  Raiffeisen Bank International | Member of RBI Group | Financial Year 2024   The biodervistity policy  is available on Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.’s website. 
E4-3: Actions and resources related to biodiversity and ecosystems
In a first step, RBI started by developing a biodiversity-focused materiality assessment for the loan portfolio in 2024, the 
conclusions of which will be reflected accordingly by the internal steering. In addition, RBI will define the data required for it to 
take a more in-depth approach towards biodiversity and allow it to set quantitative targets. 
The RBI biodiversity policy is to be completed  in 2025 , in order to subsequently derive actions and targets from the identified 
risks and opportunities. 
Value chain
RBI has been working on (re)defining its approach to industries that have a negative impact on biodiversity by further 
developing sector-specific group policies. 
For further information see chapter  Sector policies . 
Actions for assets under management
A biodiversity position paper was published in 2024 by Raiffeisen Kapitalanlage-Gesellschaft m.b.H.  This paper is aimed at 
initiating the journey towards incorporating biodiversity and nature-related impacts, risks and dependencies in organizational 
processes on a portfolio level. In the course of 2024, five initiation targets  addressing the commitments of the Finance for 
Biodiversity Pledge were established and disclosed. These commitments can be achieved by collaborating and sharing 
knowledge, engaging with companies, assessing impact, setting targets and reporting publicly by end of 2025 . 
The current assets in scope of this policy refer to holdings of corporate issuers of self-managed mutual funds. 
E4-4: Targets related to biodiversity and ecosystems
Value chain
After finalizing the Biodiversity Policy, which serves to identify the risks and opportunities, and establish the course of action 
regarding measures to be taken, RBI will focus on setting biodiversity targets in 2025 and 2026. 
E4-5: Impact metrics related to biodiversity and ecosystems change
Value chain
After finalizing the Biodiversity Policy , which serves to identify the risks and opportunities as well as establish the course of 
action regarding measures and target setting, RBI will also define impac t parameters for biodiversity in 2025 and 2026.

E5-1 : Policies related to resource use and circular economy
Value chain
As a rule, RBI’s approach to sustainable business practices is covered in the c limate and environmental business strategy . Due 
to the impact on a bank’s risk assessment, environmental topics such as resource use and circular economy are also included in 
RBI’s risk framework ( see chapter Climate change ). Furthermore, RBI is implementing sectoral strategies to define supportive, 
transformative and restrictive criteria, including climate and circular economy aspects.
The targets and actions for the central topics of climate stability and circularity were defined by the business areas. These 
were implemented in sectoral business  policies  such as oil & gas, steel and real estate & construction.
RBI has also been working on (re)defining its approach to industries with high CO 2 emissions and/or high negative impacts on 
circularity and biodiversity by further developing sector-specific Group policies. 
For more details see chapter  RBI’s climate and environmental business strategy . 
Own operations
Circularity and resource efficiency in RBI’s own operations are covered in the environmental policy. RBI is actively working on 
reducing the consumption of material and increasing awareness among employees about reuse and recycling. Considerations 
of resource use and sustainable sourcing also influence the relationship with RBI’s suppliers (see G1-2: Management of 
relationships with suppliers ). 
For more details RBI refers to the environmental policy  and RBI supplier code of conduct . 
E5-2 : Actions and resources related to resource use and circular economy
Value chain
From a steering perspective, the E-score (an important component of the total ESG score) is already reflected in how RBI 
clusters its customers. RBI has therefore set up the underwriting process to include the ESG component. As a result, circularity 
also plays an indirect role. Further developments in this area will be considered in 2025, as additional quantitative KPIs may be 
needed.
As part of the climate and environmental business strategy, which focuses on supporting RBI’s customers in their sustainable 
transition, RBI provides in-depth advisory services on net-zero strategy and circularity topics. 
In 2024, RBI saw an increase in the volume of business compared to the previous year. This stems from the financing of 
circularity projects, where the focal point is developing  eco-efficient products and production activities that enhance resource 
efficiency, as well as projects that relate to waste prevention, waste reduction and waste recycling. 
In terms of circularity, figures on waste and material consumption have been determined and analyzed as part of a KPI 
calculation since 2016. To better address the negative impact on circularity, RBI has been an active member of the PRB 
Resource Efficiency and Circularity Target working group set up by UNEP FI since since 2022. 
To improve data collection in this area, circularity is included in the RBI ESG questionnaire as one of the main environmental 
aspects. 
Own operations
Actions concerning the improvement of circularity and reduction of resource use in RBI’s own operations are taken by local 
Facility Management and Procurement officers, and are aligned with Group ESG & Sustainability Management. These actions 
range from switching from plastic bottles to glass, reducing paper consumption and increasing the waste recycling quota.
Furthermore, RBI continues with its efforts to prolong the use of IT equipment (mobile phones, laptops,...) and encourage its re-
use once it is no longer required within the company.The number of IT equipment items procured per quarter in 2024, as well as 
equipment items leaving the company through reuse programs, are tracked internally. While RBI has to take into account 
technical constraints and security requirements, efforts are being made to reduce resource intake and maximize the usability 
of materials. 
The actions support RBI’s overall environmental goals and targets for energy efficiency and reduction of CO 2 emissions outlined 
in chapter Climate change . Group management report                                                                                                                                                    339

title: Resource use and circular economy
summary:
- Scope and governance: The section outlines RBI’s approach to resource use and circular economy across its value chain and own operations, anchored in its climate and environmental business strategy and risk framework. Sectoral strategies/policies (e.g., oil & gas, steel, real estate & construction) define supportive, transformative, and restrictive criteria, with ongoing refinement for high-CO2 and high-impact sectors. Own-operations circularity is governed by an environmental policy and supplier engagement via the Supplier Code of Conduct.

- Actions in the value chain: RBI integrates an ESG E-score into customer clustering and underwriting, giving circularity an indirect role. It provides advisory services on net-zero and circularity, and increased financing in 2024 for circularity projects (eco-efficient products, resource-efficient production, waste prevention/reduction/recycling). Waste and material KPIs have been tracked since 2016. RBI participates in the UNEP FI PRB Resource Efficiency and Circularity Target working group (since 2022) and includes circularity in its ESG questionnaire.

- Actions in own operations: Local Facility Management and Procurement, aligned with Group ESG & Sustainability, implement measures such as switching from plastic to glass, reducing paper, raising recycling rates, extending IT hardware lifecycles, and promoting reuse. IT procurement and reuse volumes are tracked quarterly, balancing technical and security constraints to reduce resource intake.

- Targets in the value chain: Circular economy is a UN PRB focal area, with initial priority on packaging and building materials. For packaging, RBI aligns with the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (70% recycling by 2030) and material-specific targets, and has set:
  - By 2030: Relevant packaging-industry customers’ post-consumer packaging waste recycled per the Directive.
  - By 2028: Circularity topics included in at least 90% of customer engagements in the packaging sector.
  RBI is guided by the EU Taxonomy for construction materials and plans to set portfolio-level targets in 2025.

- Targets in own operations: Circularity targets support overall emissions-reduction goals, focusing on material use (notably IT and business travel) and waste. Implementation is driven by an ISO 14001-certified environmental management system (since 1998) and ISO 14064-1:2019 GHG validation for head office (since 2013), overseen by the Environmental Committee and ESG/sustainability teams.

- Resource inflows (value chain): Portfolio impacts on resource intensity are analyzed using the UNEP FI impact tool; key drivers are real estate, land transport (including pipelines), and electricity/gas/steam/air conditioning supply.

- Resource inflows (own operations): Primary physical inputs include office supplies, IT equipment, and company cars; energy is a critical input covered elsewhere. Procurement emphasizes environmental and social sustainability. Purchased goods/services (including cloud) are reported in Scope 3 emissions, with all material goods recorded quarterly.

- Resource outflows: Addressed in conjunction with resource inflows per ESRS linkage, with cross-references to related chapters.

- Data, monitoring, and alignment: Ongoing KPI development (potentially adding quantitative circularity metrics in 2025), regular internal tracking, and alignment with broader climate goals and regulatory frameworks (EU directives and taxonomy).

As part of RBI’s commitment to the UN Principles for Responsible Banking, it has identified the circular economy as a key focal 
area. Based on the impact analysis, RBI has initially given priority to the packaging and building materials sectors. 
For packaging, RBI is aligning its efforts with the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive 94/62/EC, which mandates that

presented by the circular economy, and explore financial incentives and support mechanisms, to facilitate this transition to a 
green economy.

Own operations

and business travel) and waste contribute significantly to RBI’s CO2 footprint. It is therefore in RBI’s interest to continually work 
on reducing the environmental impact stemming from resource use. 
A central tool for the implementation and further development of the environmental targets is the environmental 
management system in Austria, which is operated in accordance with the requirements of ISO 14001 (certified since 1998). In

title: Social Information
summary:
- Scope: Social information on RBI’s own workforce under ESRS, covering both employees and non‑employees.
- Strategic framing (ESRS 2 SBM‑3): The workforce is integral to RBI’s Strategic Roadmap 2024–2025; goal to be an attractive employer with a high‑performing culture.
- People and culture priorities: leadership development; fostering a collaborative, customer‑centric culture; building current and future capabilities; sustainable and fair reward and recognition; strong employer branding; meaningful careers and growth; emphasis on continuous learning and high qualification standards in a regulated industry.
- Working conditions and employee relations: focus on high employee satisfaction and secure employment; benefits extended to part‑time and temporary staff; acknowledgment that job security influences financial stability, health, stress, and work‑life balance.
- Non‑employee workforce: use of service‑contract providers and temporary agency workers; RBI defines tasks for agency temps; specific note of agency‑engaged IT staff at Raiffeisenbank a.s. (Prague) and Raiffeisen Bank Sh.a (Tirana).
- Early‑career/temporary programs: seasonal trainees (June–October, 1–4 months, pupils and students, supportive/administrative tasks without independent responsibility) and internships (up to 6 months with possible extension, enrolled students, similar supportive tasks); both offered full‑time.
- Impact lens: recognition of both positive and negative impacts of workforce practices on operations.

ESRS 2 SBM-3: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with 
strategy  and business model
Positive and negative impacts (own operations)
The importance of the own workforce for own operations is evident in the fact that the  Group Strateg ic Roadmap  for 2024 and 
2025 includes RBI’s approach towards its own workforce (hereinafter people and culture) as a distinct point. RBI has the 
objective to be an attractive employer and have a high-performing culture. The pillar of people and culture contains  in detail 
the strategic initiatives designed to equip managers to become conscious and effective leaders, to strengthen a collaborative 
and customer-centric culture, to ensure the right capabilities for now and for the future, to offer a sustainable and fair reward 
and recognition system, to be an authentic and distinctive employer, and to provide meaningful careers and growth.
RBI is aware that employees are its greatest asset. Continued success can only be achieved with satisfied, motivated, and 
healthy employees. Since working in banks is subject to high regulatory requirements and requires highly qualified employees, 
attention must be focused on well-qualified and well-trained staff who can successfully complete their assigned tasks. As a 
learning organization, RBI is aware that continuous development is necessary to maintain high standards. 
Working conditions
Employee relationships 
With regard to working conditions, high employee satisfaction is of utmost importance to RBI. As stated in the strategic 
objectives, RBI strives to be a distinctive and authentic employer and ultimately provide secure employment. Insecure or 
temporary jobs may lead to insecurity for those who are affected and prevent secure life planning, while secure employment 
offers financial stability and results in higher employee satisfaction. Therefore, RBI also offers a range of benefits for part-time 
or temporary employees. The nature of the employment relationship can also have a significant impact on an individual’s 
health, influencing factors such as stress levels and work-life balance.
Although the majority of employees have an employment contract with RBI, there are individuals who do not have an 
employment relationship with RBI but still provide services to RBI (non-employees). They primarily assist with project-related 
tasks or in times of temporary  staffing shortages. A distinction is made between individuals who come to RBI under a service 
contract between RBI and another company to provide the services defined in the service contract, and those individuals who 
have a contract with a temporary employment agency. In the latter case, RBI is responsible for defining and structuring the 
tasks. Raiffeisenbank a.s. in Prague and Raiffeisen Bank Sh.a in Tirana also have employees, primarily in the IT sector, who are 
engaged through a temporary employment agency.
During the summer months from June to October, temporary employment contracts are concluded with seasonal trainees at 
head office. The traineeships can last between one and four months and can be undertaken by both school pupils and 
university students. Their tasks include supportive and administrative activities without personal responsibility. 
Head office also offers the opportunity to conclude internship contracts. Such internships are limited to a maximum period of 
six months, with the option to extend. An individual who takes up an internship must be enrolled in a course of study. Interns 
also carry out supportive and administrative work without independent areas of responsibility. Both seasonal trainees and 
internships are offered on a full-time basis.

title: Own workforce
summary:
- Purpose and scope
  - ESRS-aligned disclosure on “Own workforce” covering employees and non-employees, with strategic importance embedded in RBI’s People & Culture pillar.
- Material impacts, risks and opportunities
  - Positive aims: attractive employer, high-performing culture, secure employment, fair reward, meaningful careers, continuous learning.
  - Potential negatives and financial risks: equal pay gaps, discrimination, weak whistleblowing, poor work-life balance—leading to operational disruption, fines, legal costs, turnover, productivity loss, and reputational harm.
- Working conditions and employment relationships
  - Predominantly permanent contracts; fixed-term only in defined cases (e.g., parental leave cover, initial 6-month period).
  - Use of seasonal trainees and internships; limited use of agency/contracted non-employees for projects or shortages.
  - Flexible working time, hybrid/telework and part-time options to support work-life balance; benefits extended broadly, with some country-specific limitations.
- Health, safety and wellbeing
  - Strong focus on physical and mental health, ergonomic workplaces, burnout prevention, health checks, wellness programs, psychological support (incl. post-robbery).
  - Group-wide H&S systems, risk-based monitoring, and monthly reviews by health@RBI.
- Fair pay and rewards
  - Group total rewards policy ensures market-adequate, primarily fixed remuneration with fully flexible variable pay; focus on financial stability and development.
  - Commitment to adequate wages and upcoming salary transparency project (EU Pay Transparency Directive).
- Employee voice and participation
  - Multiple engagement channels: CEO live calls, regular employee surveys and pulse checks, staff councils (45% coverage), European Works Council, employee reps on Supervisory Boards in several countries.
  - Ombudsperson (RBI AG) for confidential, neutral support and systemic insights.
  - Whistleblowing via Whispli platform for anonymous reporting; structured internal violation management.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI)
  - Group D&I policy, diversity officers in all key subsidiaries, employee resource groups (e.g., EMBRACE for LGBTQIA+), Board sponsorship, national diversity charters.
  - Programs for women’s empowerment, generation management, disability inclusion, intercultural topics; extensive leader and staff trainings on anti-harassment and inclusion.
  - Broad flexibility measures (hybrid, part-time, educational leave), dependent care supports, and country-specific work-family benefits.
- Learning, development and performance
  - Group policies for learning, talent management and performance; mandatory annual development dialogues; talent and trainee programs across countries.
  - ESG Academy and SkillUp! ESG journeys; AI Pioneer Program to accelerate AI literacy and adoption; leadership initiative on impactful conversations.
- Data protection and governance
  - HR GDPR policy and broader data protection rules; operational risk reporting of HR-related incidents; adherence to ILO principles and UN/EU human rights standards.
  - Company agreements in Austria on flexible working time and social benefits; periodic reviews.
- Targets and management approach
  - 2025 goals: maintain whistleblowing standards; sustain flexible/hybrid work; publish and implement updated D&I policy; develop engagement metrics; launch pay transparency project.
  - Women in senior leadership target of 35% achieved in 2024; annual goal setting cascaded across Group HR.
- Key metrics (2024, selected)
  - Workforce: 43,574 employees (17,146 male; 26,428 female); major countries—Russia 8,852; Ukraine 5,690; Austria 5,390; Romania 5,047.
  - Employment types: 40,847 permanent; 2,727 temporary; 2,629 part-time; turnover 18%.
  - Non-employees: 3,486 (agency and service-contract workers).
  - Collective arrangements: 41% covered by CBAs; 45% covered by worker representatives; EWC active.
  - Diversity: B-1 (63% male/37% female); B-2 (53% male/47% female); age—21% <30, 62% 30–50, 17% >50.
  - Social protection: Kosovo exceptions; otherwise broad coverage for sickness, unemployment, injury/disability, parental, retirement.
  - Disability: 1.48% of employees (per local legal definitions).
  - Development: 92% had performance/career reviews; average 34 training hours (31 male/36 female).
  - Health & safety: 100% coverage; 0 fatalities; 86 work-related accidents; recordable rate 1.11.
  - Work-life balance: 100% entitlement to maternity, paternity, carers’ leave; take-up—maternity 14%, paternity 1%, carers’ 1% male/6% female.
  - Pay: unadjusted Group gender pay gap 38% (27% unweighted country average); highest-to-median pay ratio 89.
  - Incidents: 4 discrimination cases; 63 complaints via channels; €0 fines; 0 severe human rights incidents.
- Effectiveness monitoring
  - Regular employee surveys, external work-family audit, ongoing health and safety reviews, and dedicated DEI/HR resources to track and refine measures.
